No and no. r = 0 only rules out linear association (quadratics, U-shapes, interactions can be strong). r measures association; causation requires design (randomization, natural experiments) or much stronger modeling assumptions.
Spearman. A single point moved Pearson’s estimate violently because r is built from raw deviations — the outlier dominates both \(s_x\), \(s_y\) and the cross-products. Spearman caps any point’s influence at “one rank step.”

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — Anscombe’s quartet, cell 1. This classic dataset has 4 pairs with (nearly) identical mean, SD, r ≈ 0.816, and regression line — utterly different shapes. Build pair I and pair III, compute their summary statistics, and plot both.


Solution







Identical r, identical fitted line — because r and OLS are single-number summaries that different data structures can satisfy. Summary statistics compress away exactly the things you care about; plotting is not optional.

Exercise 2. Construct data where adding ONE observation flips the sign of Pearson r (from negative to positive), while Spearman barely moves. Report all three r values before/after.


Solution







The added point sits at the extreme corner, contributing huge cross-deviations \((x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\) — enough to outvote 40 points. Spearman only sees “new highest x, new highest y” — one rank step on each side. Any reported Pearson on real data should come with a scatterplot or a rank-correlation cross-check.

Exercise 3. For a bivariate normal sample (n = 30, true ρ = 0), empirically show the sampling distribution of r under the null, and verify that |r| > \(2/\sqrt{n-1}\) (rough 5% rule) happens about 5% of the time.


Solution







≈ 0.05: with n = 30, “noise correlations” of ±0.37 are routine. Two implications: small-n correlation claims need formal tests (1.4), and large correlation matrices (0.3 pandas drills) will always show impressive-looking r values somewhere — that’s multiplication of opportunities, not biology.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Correlation ≠ causation — and neither correlation nor its absence is about linear vs nonlinear: r ≈ 0 coexists with perfect functional dependence (the x² plot).
Range restriction and range enhancement: selecting only high-GPA applicants lowers r; mixing two clusters inflates it (Simpson’s paradox lives here — see Complex Questions).
Pearson needs rough linearity and tolerates outliers badly; Spearman needs only monotonicity but discards magnitude information (two datasets with identical ranks can have very different practical effect sizes).
Correlation matrices in high dimensions (10,000 genes → 50M pairs): extreme r values appear by chance alone (Exercise 3 logic × opportunities). Multiple-testing discipline (Part 12) applies to “top correlated pairs” lists.
Averaging correlations across groups is invalid (r is not on an additive scale — use Fisher z, or analyze per group).
Bootstrap or Fisher-z CI for r, never “r ± 0.05” from folklore. Formal test: stats.pearsonr returns the p-value alongside.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “correlation report” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


r ≠ slope and ≠ causation. The slope estimate is np.polyfit’s job, and “causes” needs design evidence, not correlation.
Averaging r across groups is invalid and hides sign flips; here group r’s may be +1 and −1, “averaging” to 0 while both groups have perfect (opposite) associations. Report per-group r (or Fisher-z average with justification).
r ≈ 0 ≠ no relationship. The U-shaped dependence is perfect; Pearson only tests the linear projection.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that for simple linear regression the fitted slope is \(b = r \cdot (s_y / s_x)\), and explain the two failure modes of “reading” r as if it were an effect size.


Hint

Write the OLS slope for standardized variables; then unstandardize.



Solution

Standardize both variables: \(\tilde x = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(\tilde y = (y-\bar y)/s_y\). For standardized data the OLS slope is \(\sum \tilde x_i \tilde y_i / \sum \tilde x_i^2 = (n-1)\,\text{cov}/(n-1)\,\text{var} = r\). Rescaling back multiplies by \(s_y/s_x\), giving \(b = r s_y/s_x\). Failure modes: (1) slope from r — r = 0.5 means nothing about units; a weak correlation with huge \(s_y/s_x\) can be a big effect. (2) r as slope — the same physical relationship yields different r if you restrict the x-range (range restriction lowers both spread and r) while the slope \(r s_y/s_x\) is more stable. Report both: r (strength of linear association), slope (effect per unit x), CI each.

Q2. The t-statistic for testing ρ = 0 is \(t = r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\). Verify numerically that stats.pearsonr’s p-value matches the two-sided t-test with df = n−2, then explain what happens to that p-value’s meaning when you compute it for the largest of 10,000 gene-pair correlations.


Solution







The p-value is calibrated for one pre-specified pair. For the maximum over 10,000 pairs, the test is applied to the extreme order statistic of ~10,000 correlated tests: even under global null, the smallest p-value is routinely ≪ 0.05 (probability of at least one “significant” pair ≈ 1 − 0.95¹⁰⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 1). The honest procedure re-tests the selected pair in fresh data or applies family-wise/FDR correction — the entire subject of Part 12.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (relationships × 0.3 pandas — Simpson’s paradox). Build 3 groups where within every group r(y, x) is positive, but pooled over all groups r is strongly negative. (Give group intercepts very different levels and equal within-group slopes.) Then answer: which correlation should a model use — and how does adding group dummies (2.6 Categorical predictors) resolve the conflict?
C2 (relationships × 9.2 PCA preview). Generate 3 correlated variables, compute the correlation matrix, and its eigenvalues. What does the dominant eigenvalue/eigenvector tell you about how many “real directions” the data has? Relate this to why the scatter-matrix drill of 0.4 becomes unreadable at 50 variables and PCA becomes necessary.

title: 1.2 Relationships Between Variables
text:
7. Summary

Covariance is direction × scale; Pearson r standardizes it to [−1, 1]; Spearman replaces values with ranks.
r describes linear association only: U-shapes hide at r ≈ 0; monotone curves lose r < 1.
r² is explained-variance for a straight line; slope is r·(sy/sx) — never confuse strength with effect size.
One outlier can flip Pearson; Spearman caps that influence — report both when data is dirty.
Sampling noise gives |r| ≈ 0.3 routinely at n = 30; scanning many pairs manufactures “discoveries.”
Per-group correlation, plots, and range questions come before any causal sentence.
Association is a description; deciding whether a pattern would reappear in new samples requires probability and inference — 1.3 Probability essentials.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text: Descriptive statistics compress a sample into a few honest numbers: where is the center, how wide is the spread, what shape is the distribution. Every model diagnostic, every “significant difference,” every anomaly alert you will ever compute rests on these primitives — so the definitions (including the ones with silent variants, like population vs sample SD) must be reflexes.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
1. Basic Concept
Center. The mean \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i\) is the balance point; the median is the middle value by rank. They coincide for symmetric data; for right-skewed data, mean > median (a few large values drag the mean).
Spread. The variance is the average squared deviation from the mean. Two flavors:
\[s^2_{\text{pop}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \qquad s^2_{\text{sample}} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\]
The \(n-1\) (Bessel’s correction) in the sample version compensates for the fact that \(\bar{x}\) was estimated from the same data — deviations from an estimated center are systematically too small. Standard deviation is the square root, back in data units.






Position and shape. Quartiles split the sorted data into quarters; the IQR (Q3 − Q1) is the spread of the middle half — robust to outliers. Skewness measures asymmetry (positive = right tail).






Robustness ranking (how much a single extreme value can move the statistic):

mean, SD — sensitive (breakdown point 0%)
median, IQR — robust (breakdown point 50%)
trimmed mean — tunable middle ground

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the sample variance divide by \(n-1\) instead of \(n\)?
Your gene-expression distribution has mean 210 and median 85. What shape do you suspect, and which two numbers would you report?
Is the IQR affected by multiplying all values by 10? By adding one extreme value?
When is the mode the most informative measure of center?
What does ddof=0 vs ddof=1 change in np.std, and which does pandas use by default?



Answers


Deviations are taken from the sample mean, which is itself fitted to the data; the fitted center absorbs part of the variability, shrinking deviations. Dividing by the degrees of freedom \(n-1\) unbias the estimate of the population variance (for normal data, exactly).
Strong right skew (a minority of very high values). Report median and IQR (robust pair); if you must report the mean, report it with the median so the skew is visible.
Multiplying by 10: IQR scales by 10 (it’s in data units). One extreme value beyond the fences: IQR is unaffected as long as it doesn’t cross the 25th/75th percentiles — that’s the point of quartile-based spread.
For categorical or discrete data (“most common category”), and for multimodal continuous data where mean and median both describe nothing real (“typical patient: bimodal, modes at X and Y”).
ddof = delta degrees of freedom subtracted from n. ddof=0 → population formula; ddof=1 → sample formula. NumPy defaults to 0, pandas to 1 — mixing pandas and NumPy without noticing this is a classic silent bug.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Write summarize(x) returning {"n", "mean", "sd", "median", "iqr", "min", "max"} using sample SD. Test it on normal data and on lognormal data; state which summary number changes most between the two and why.


Solution







The mean and SD blow up under lognormal data (they inherit the heavy tail), while median and IQR stay near their symmetric-data values — the empirical demonstration of robustness. Report median/IQR for skewed data.

Exercise 2. IQR outlier rule: flag values outside \([Q_1 - 1.5\,\text{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\text{IQR}]\) in the dataset below. Then compute z-scores and flag \(|z| > 3\). Compare the flagged sets and explain the disagreement.


Solution







The z-score rule uses the mean and SD — which the outlier itself inflates. One extreme value widened the SD so much that even the outlier isn’t 3 SDs out (masking). Quartile-based rules don’t have this self-blinding property: for small samples, prefer the IQR fence.

Exercise 3. Empirically verify Bessel’s correction: sample n = 5 points from a known distribution many times; for each sample compute variance with ddof=0 and ddof=1; average each. Which average converges to the true variance?


Solution







ddof=0 averages to \(0.8\sigma^2\) here (\((n-1)/n = 4/5\)) — a 20% underestimate, every time, silently. This is why the divisor choice is not a technicality.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

pandas vs NumPy ddof defaults disagree (pandas std/var use ddof=1; NumPy uses ddof=0). Numbers in mixed reports can differ by ~√(n/(n−1)) for no reason.
NaN handling differs: np.mean poisons, np.nanmean skips, pandas .mean() skips and warns differently — know which behavior produced a reported number.
Percentile interpolation: np.percentile linearly interpolates by default; small-n quartiles depend on this convention (9 conventions exist; R’s type=7 matches NumPy’s linear).
SD is not the “typical deviation” for skewed data: with a heavy right tail, most deviations are below the SD. IQR communicates spread more honestly there.
The mean minimizes squared error, the median absolute error — which is why least squares regression (Part 2) is mean-focused and least-absolutes-deviations is median-focused.
stats.mode behavior changed across SciPy versions (now returns a ModeResult object); pd.Series.mode is the stable, readable choice.
Descriptives ≠ inference: a summary is a claim about this sample; Part 1.4 is about claims regarding the population.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated summary function has three bugs. Run it on the test data and find them.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Population SD (ddof=0) — for a sample summary this underestimates spread; specify and use ddof=1.
No NaN policy — the function dies on the NaN (mean → nan, max → nan) without telling the caller whether NaNs were dropped. Make the policy explicit.
range on data containing NaN raises/propagates nan; also “range” is a fragile descriptives choice (a single typo’d value sets it) — min/max separately at most, or a robust span.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove (or verify by simulation) that the sample mean is the value \(c\) minimizing \(\sum_i (x_i - c)^2\), and the sample median minimizes \(\sum_i |x_i - c|\). What does each say about which errors the mean vs median take most seriously?


Hint

Differentiate \(\sum (x_i-c)^2\) in \(c\); for the absolute value, argue by moving \(c\) across data points and counting how many terms’ slope changes.



Solution

Mean: \(f(c)=\sum(x_i-c)^2\) has \(f'(c) = -2\sum(x_i-c)\), zero exactly at \(c=\bar{x}\) (second derivative \(2n>0\)). Median: \(g(c)=\sum|x_i-c|\) has slope \(= (\#\,\text{points} < c) - (\#\,\text{points} > c)\), which changes sign where the counts balance — the median. So the mean’s optimality is defined in squared error: a single far point contributes quadratically, dominating the objective — hence the mean chases outliers. The median’s objective is linear in each error: one far point costs the same as one near point — hence its robustness. This one paragraph explains robust statistics, why least-squares regression is outlier-sensitive, and why quantile regression exists.

Q2. Two labs each report SD ≈ 2.0 for the same assay. Lab A ran n = 5, Lab B ran n = 5,000. Construct a scenario where both reports are true, and explain which additional number distinguishes them (preview: it is not the SD).


Solution

Both labs can honestly report \(s \approx 2.0\) — SD describes individual measurement spread and barely depends on n. What distinguishes them is the precision of their estimated means: the standard error \(s/\sqrt{n}\) ≈ 0.89 for Lab A vs 0.028 for Lab B — a 30-fold difference. SD answers “how noisy is one measurement,” SE answers “how well do I know the center.” Confusing the two (reporting SD where SE is meant, or vice versa) is a notorious publication bug; the inference machinery that formalizes it arrives in 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (descriptives × 0.4 EDA). For the lognormal samples from Section 1, produce side-by-side: (a) histogram of x, (b) histogram of log x with a normal-density overlay scaled to the log data. Which single transformation converts all the robust-vs-sensitive summary disagreements (mean/median, SD/IQR) into non-issues, and what does that imply about when those disagreements matter?
C2 (descriptives × 3.1.5 AUPRC preview). A screening cohort has 1% disease prevalence. Compute the mean/median of the binary label vector and explain, in descriptive-statistics language, why accuracy is a nearly useless summary for a classifier on this data (predicting all-healthy scores 99%). Which descriptive statistic of the confusion matrix would you report instead, and why is it robust to the prevalence imbalance?

title: 1.1 Descriptive Statistics
text:
7. Summary

Center: mean (balance, sensitive) vs median (rank, robust); skew shows as mean − median.
Spread: SD for symmetric data, IQR for skewed; ddof=0 vs 1 is a real bias, and pandas/NumPy disagree by default.
Quartiles + IQR fences detect outliers without being blinded by them; z-scores can be.
NaN policy is part of the statistic: nan-skipping is a decision, not a default to trust blindly.
Mean ↔︎ squared error, median ↔︎ absolute error: robustness follows from the loss function.
SD describes single measurements; SE describes the precision of a mean — next pages formalize this.
Summaries describe samples; to argue about populations you need probability and inference: 1.2 Relationships first asks how two variables move together.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text: Probability is the language in which every model speaks: a predicted probability, a p-value, a 95% interval, a likelihood. This page drills the rules, the three distributions that do most of the work in ML (binomial, Poisson, normal), and the one formula — Bayes’ rule — that most people’s intuition gets wrong.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
1. Basic Concept
The rules. For events A and B:

Complement: \(P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)\) — “at least one” questions become “1 minus none.”
Addition: \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\) — the intersection is counted twice, subtract once.
Multiplication / conditioning: \(P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)\); independence means \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), so for independent events conditioning changes nothing.
Bayes: \(P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}\) — the flip between “evidence given cause” and “cause given evidence.”







Random variables and their machines. A distribution assigns probability to outcomes. The three workhorses:









Distribution
Models
Parameters
scipy




Binomial
# successes in n independent yes/no trials
n, p
stats.binom


Poisson
# events in fixed time/space (counts, reads)
λ (rate)
stats.poisson


Normal
sums/averages of many small effects (CLT)
μ, σ
stats.norm









Expectation and variance are the distribution’s center and spread: \(E[X] = \sum x\,p(x)\); for the sum of independent variables, means add and variances add (this additive rule powers everything from portfolio risk to the SE of a mean).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
2. Concept Questions

A test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific; prevalence is 1/1000. Roughly what fraction of positive results are true positives, and which two quantities fought each other in the Bayes computation?
When does Poisson model counts well, and what does it assume that binomial does not?
What is P(X = 4.0) for a continuous random variable, and what do we evaluate instead?
Why do variances add but standard deviations don’t?
If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.8, what is P(A ∪ B)?



Answers


About 9%. The fight: the evidence actually observed (true positives, \(0.99 \times 0.001\)) versus the much larger pool of false positives generated by the huge healthy majority (\(0.01 \times 0.999\)). Base rate dominates when prevalence is low.
Poisson fits counts of events in a fixed window when events are rare and independent (reads overlapping a gene, mutations per kb). It assumes events occur with a constant rate and no upper bound; binomial counts successes in a fixed number of trials n.
Zero — a point has no width, so its probability mass is 0. We evaluate \(P(X \le x)\) (CDF) or \(P(a < X < b)\) (density integrated over the interval).
Variance adds because the cross-terms of independent variables average to zero: \(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X)+\text{Var}(Y)\). SD is the square root of that sum, and square roots don’t add: \(\sqrt{a+b} \ne \sqrt a + \sqrt b\).
\(P(A\cup B) = 0.5 + 0.8 - 0.5\times0.8 = 0.9\).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1 — the full Bayes computation. Disease prevalence 0.1%, test sensitivity 99%, specificity 99%. Compute (a) P(disease | positive), (b) the same for prevalence 10%, (c) how high specificity must be at 0.1% prevalence for PPV ≥ 50%. State each result as one sentence.


Solution








9% — a positive result is usually false at 0.1% prevalence. (b) 92% — the same test is excellent in a high-risk population. (c) specificity ≈ 99.90% — the false-positive rate per healthy person must be driven below the true prevalence. Same machine, three different decisions — this is why screening policies depend on prevalence, not just on test quality.


Exercise 2 — Monte Carlo verification. Verify analytically-computed probabilities by simulation: (a) at least one six in 4 rolls; (b) P(Binomial(20, 0.3) ≥ 10); (c) P(Normal(0,1) within ±1.5). Report simulated vs exact to 3 decimals.


Solution







Note the pattern — sf(9, ...) for “≥ 10” (sf is P(X > k), so use k−1). Monte Carlo with N = 10⁶ carries ~0.05% MC error; agreement to 3 decimals is expected, and this verify-by-simulation habit will debug countless probability computations later.

Exercise 3 — the law of total probability in a lab setting. 1% of samples are contaminated. Contaminated samples fail QC 80% of the time; clean samples fail 2% of the time. What fraction of samples fail QC? Given a sample failed QC, what’s the probability it was contaminated?


Solution







Two-step structure: total probability pools the failure rate across the two sample types; Bayes re-weights to ask about the cause. Even a 40× higher failure rate for contaminated samples only gets you to 27% — because clean samples are 99× more numerous. Always ask what population produced this positive.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

P(A|B) vs P(B|A) — transposing the conditional is the prosecutor’s fallacy; DNA-match statistics are its most famous victim. Every Bayes computation should start by naming which conditional you have and which you want.
Independence is not “small correlation” and not “no obvious relationship” — it is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\) exactly. Rarely true for biological measurements (batch, relatedness, shared environment).
pdf values are not probabilities — stats.norm.pdf(0) ≈ 0.4 yet P(X=0) = 0; the density integrates to probability. Only CDFs and intervals carry probability meaning.
sf(k) = P(X > k) (strictly greater) — the classic off-by-one: P(X ≥ 10) = sf(9), not sf(10). Write the inequality before writing the function call.
Poisson has variance = mean; real count data routinely violates this (overdispersion) — the reason negative-binomial models exist in RNA-seq DE analysis (12.6).
CLT applies to standardized sums of many independent contributions — not to heavy-tailed data at small n, and not to highly skewed counts at n = 5.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “screening calculator” has three bugs. Run it, then fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Complement misuse: the stray “× 3” multiplies the none-detect probability by 3, producing a negative “probability”. The complement of “at least one” is “none”, full stop: \(1 - 0.9^3\).
sf off-by-one: sf(8) = P(X > 8) = P(X ≥ 9); for P(X ≥ 8) use sf(7).
pdf differences are not probabilities — subtracting densities is meaningless. Integrate: cdf(1.96) - cdf(-1.96).

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the 9% PPV result symbolically and explain in terms of the Bayes numerator and denominator why increasing sensitivity barely helps at low prevalence, while increasing specificity helps enormously.


Hint

Write PPV \(= \frac{sp\,\pi}{sp\,\pi + (1-sc)(1-\pi)}\) and ask: which term shrinks when sens ↑ vs spec ↑, at \(\pi = 0.001\)?



Solution

PPV \(= \dfrac{\text{sens}\cdot\pi}{\text{sens}\cdot\pi + (1-\text{spec})(1-\pi)}\). At \(\pi = 0.001\): the numerator term is ≈ sens × 0.001 — small no matter how good sens is (bounded by prevalence itself). The denominator’s second term is \((1-\text{spec}) \times 0.999\) — nearly the whole healthy population times the false-positive rate. Raising sens 0.99 → 0.999 multiplies the numerator by ~1.009; raising spec 0.99 → 0.999 divides the false-positive term by 10. At low prevalence, PPV is governed by specificity — which is why screening programs chase specificity and why confirmatory (more specific) tests follow any positive screen.

Q2. Two independent watchtowers detect fires with probabilities 0.8 and 0.7 respectively. Given exactly one detection occurred, what is the probability it was tower 1? Compute symbolically and verify by Monte Carlo.


Hint

Enumerate the four detection outcomes with their probabilities; condition on the two “exactly one” outcomes.



Solution

Outcomes: both \(= 0.8 \times 0.7 = 0.56\); neither \(= 0.2 \times 0.3 = 0.06\); only-1 \(= 0.8 \times 0.3 = 0.24\); only-2 \(= 0.2 \times 0.7 = 0.14\). Given “exactly one”, it was tower 1 with probability \(0.24/(0.24 + 0.14) = 0.632\).






Note the method: enumerate + condition, or simulate — both beat formula-hunting when the event structure gets any more complicated.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (probability × 0.5 Data splitting). A test set has n = 50 samples with true accuracy p = 0.8. Compute the exact probability (binomial) that the measured accuracy is ≥ 0.9 (i.e., ≥ 45 correct). Now compute the same for n = 500. What does each number say about the credibility of “90% accuracy!” claims at the two sample sizes — and connect this to the binomial SE formula used in 0.5 Q2.
C2 (probability × 12.4 FDR preview). You test 10,000 genes for differential expression at α = 0.05; none are truly differential. (a) How many false positives do you expect? (b) What’s the probability of at least one? (c) If 100 are truly differential with 80% power, what is the positive predictive value of your “significant” list? This single calculation is the entire motivation for FDR correction — predict what q-values do before learning them.

title: 1.3 Probability Essentials
text:
7. Summary

Complement turns “at least one” into “1 − none”; addition subtracts the double-counted intersection.
Conditional probability is the primary object; independence is \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\), not an adjective.
Bayes’ rule converts P(evidence|cause) to P(cause|evidence); at low prevalence, specificity dominates PPV.
Binomial = n trials; Poisson = counts in a window (variance = mean); Normal = the CLT’s destination.
pdf values are densities, not probabilities; CDF/sf carry probability, and sf is P(X > k) — mind the off-by-one.
Variances add for independent sums; SDs don’t.
Verify any analytic probability with a Monte Carlo one-liner — cheap, and it catches unit/interval bugs.
With probability as the language, the next step is the sentence structure of statistics: estimation and testing — 1.4 Statistical inference.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text: Real predictors are often labels: tissue type, treatment arm, batch, site. Regression is numeric machinery, so categories must become numbers first — dummy (indicator) variables. Get the encoding right and everything from 2.5 applies unchanged; get it wrong and you build the classic dummy-variable trap.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
1. Basic Concept
A categorical predictor with \(k\) levels enters the model as \(k - 1\) dummy columns: each is a 0/1 flag for one level, with one level left out as the baseline (reference). The coefficients are offsets from the baseline:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_{\text{B}} + \beta_2 D_{\text{C}} + \varepsilon\]
means: group A (baseline) has mean \(\beta_0\); groups B and C are shifted by \(\beta_1, \beta_2\) from A. Why \(k-1\), not \(k\)? With all \(k\) dummies plus an intercept, the columns sum to the intercept column — perfect collinearity (2.5) — the dummy variable trap.






Reading: intercept = normal (baseline) mean; each tumor coefficient = offset from normal. Verify against group means — they must match exactly (this model is just three group means):






The same encoding, done manually — so the machinery has no mystery:

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
2. Concept Questions

A variable season has 4 levels. How many dummy columns in a model with intercept? Without intercept?
You change the baseline from “control” to “drugB”. Which numbers in the output change, which stay identical, and which scientific conclusions may change?
A colleague encodes low/medium/high severity as 0/1/2 and enters it linearly. What exactly does that assume, and when is it acceptable?
Why is the p-value of the baseline level never in the coefficient table, and how do you test whether the categorical variable matters as a whole?
pd.get_dummies without drop_first=True inside a model with intercept — what happens, and why did statsmodels’ C() not trap you?



Answers


3 with intercept (one baseline absorbed), 4 without (each level gets its own mean, no baseline needed — the “cell-means” parameterization).
Coefficients (now offsets from drugB) and the intercept change; fitted values, R², F-test, residuals are identical — same model space. Conclusions change only if you were interpreting the baseline-specific contrasts: pairwise comparisons are recomputed, the model’s fit is untouched.
It assumes equal spacing of effects per step and a monotone linear trend: high−medium = medium−low. Acceptable when the ordinal scale is genuinely near-evenly spaced in effect (or you only need a trend test); otherwise lose nothing by dummies (k−1 columns) and gain freedom.
The baseline has no coefficient — it is the intercept (its p-value tests whether the baseline mean is 0, almost never the question). To test the variable overall: the F-test dropping all its dummies (anova_lm(reduced, full) from 2.5), or a likelihood-ratio test.
With all k dummies + intercept, columns are collinear (sum of dummies = 1 = intercept) — the trap; OLS is non-identified and software either errors or silently arbitrary-solves. C() automatically leaves out the (alphabetically) first level. If you build dummies manually, drop_first=True (or drop one yourself) is the discipline.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the three-tissue dataset, run the analysis three ways: (a) C(tissue) with default baseline, (b) explicit Treatment(reference=...) choosing “tumorB”, (c) no-intercept cell-means (expr ~ C(tissue) - 1). Show that all three produce identical fitted values and R², and write out the pairwise mean differences implied by (b)’s coefficients to verify they agree with (a) after arithmetic.


Solution







One model space, three parameterizations. (c) is the most readable (coefficients are group means) but loses the baseline-contrast SEs; (a)/(b) make specific contrasts cheap. Choose the parameterization whose default outputs are the contrasts you care about.

Exercise 2 — ANOVA connection. One-way ANOVA is exactly the categorical-predictor regression above. Verify it: run smf.ols("expr ~ C(tissue)"), then compute the F-statistic for “tissue matters” three ways — (a) the model’s overall F when tissue is the only predictor, (b) anova_lm comparing with/without the factor, (c) a one-way ANOVA (statsmodels.stats.oneway.anova_oneway or scipy f_oneway). All three must agree.


Solution







Regression is the general machine; ANOVA is the special case where every predictor is categorical. Learning them as one object (rather than two rituals) pays off the moment you mix numeric + categorical predictors — which plain ANOVA cannot do.

Exercise 3. Mix numeric and categorical: fit expr ~ age + C(tissue) on the extended cohort below. Interpret each coefficient in one subject-matter sentence, then produce predicted means for each tissue at age = 50 by hand from the coefficients and verify against get_prediction. Finally, explain what this model assumes about the age effect across tissues — and name the page where that assumption gets relaxed.


Solution







The model assumes the same age slope in every tissue — parallel age-lines, offset by tissue. Whether that holds is exactly the interaction question: 2.7 Interaction terms.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Baseline choice is a reporting decision: choose the level your audience contrasts against (control/healthy), not whatever comes first alphabetically. Software defaults will happily make “drug” the baseline and “placebo” the contrast.
The dummy-variable trap is the most common hand-built-design bug: all k dummies + intercept. With get_dummies, pass drop_first=True for modeling (keep the full version for display).
Unseen levels at predict time: a category in test data that never appeared in training has no coefficient — sklearn OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown=“infrequent_if_exist”) vs silent NaN in statsmodels. Plan for level drift in productionized models.
High-cardinality categories (patient ID, gene symbol with 20k levels) explode the design matrix — target encoding or hierarchical/mixed models are the remedies, not 20k dummies.
Ordinal ≠ nominal: if order is meaningful and roughly evenly spaced in effect, a single 0/1/2 column can be more parsimonious; but always compare against the k−1 dummy version — the data, not the codebook, decides.
Interactions with dummies are the natural next step: they let each group have its own slope — precisely 2.7.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Numeric codes impose fake arithmetic: the model fits a line through codes 0,1,2 — assuming C = 2×B’s effect and ordering the labels. With nominal categories this is meaningless structure. Fix: dummies via C(site) (or justify numeric coding only for genuinely ordinal, evenly spaced scales).
All three dummies + intercept = singular design (rank deficiency; the trap). statsmodels’ pinv silently absorbs one level — non-reproducible parameterization. Fix: drop_first=True or formula C(site).
“Baseline has no effect” misreads the parameterization: A’s level is in the intercept; the tested contrasts are B−A and C−A. To ask “does site matter at all”, F-test the dummies jointly.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove that encoding k categories with k−1 dummies + intercept spans exactly the same space of fitted values as k separate group means, and that the OLS fit in both parameterizations assigns each group its own sample mean. What does this imply about residuals, R², and the model’s assumptions?


Hint

Write the design matrix; show each row picks out one group’s parameter; the least-squares problem decomposes per group.



Solution

Every observation’s prediction is “its group’s parameter” in both parameterizations, so the column space is the set of piecewise-constant-on-groups vectors — dimension k in both (k−1 dummies + intercept ≡ k cell means). RSS minimization decouples by group: within group g, minimize \(\sum_{i \in g}(y_i - c_g)^2\), solved by \(\bar y_g\). Hence identical fitted values, residuals, RSS, R², and zero within-group structure assumed — this model makes no assumptions beyond “each group has a mean”; it cannot express group-specific slopes (no numeric predictors interacting) or shared trends. That’s why adding a numeric predictor to dummies (Exercise 3) is a genuine modeling step, and letting the numeric slope vary by group is 2.7.

Q2. A collaborator fits y ~ C(biobank_site) on 40 sites and finds two sites with p < 0.05 offset coefficients, then reports “site effects identified.” Critique using 1.4 and 2.5: what family-wise issue arises, what does the joint F-test say and why does it differ, and design the defensible analysis (which test, which correction, which plot).


Solution


Selection + multiplicity: picking the 2 of 40 site coefficients with p < 0.05 is examining 40 contrasts; even under all-null, expect ~2 “hits” — exactly what was found. The per-coefficient p-values are unconditional; post-hoc selected ones need correction (Tukey/Bonferroni across site contrasts, or FDR). (b) The joint F-test (drop all 39 dummies) tests “any site differences” with one honest alpha; if it’s non-significant, the two “hits” are almost surely noise — the joint test pools all the site information and is the primary test. (c) Defensible: report the joint F (and effect-size spread of site offsets, e.g. SD of BLUPs), then if interest persists in specific sites, test those pre-specified contrasts with multiplicity correction; plot site offsets with their CIs (forest/ caterpillar plot) rather than asterisk-hunting a coefficient table. Mechanistically note also that with many small sites, individual SEs are large — significance at tiny sites is fragile by construction.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (categorical × 2.5 confounding). Simulate a study where treatment assignment depends on site (site 1 gives drug 80% of the time, site 3 gives 20%) and the drug effect is homogeneous. Show that (a) the naive drug coefficient is confounded, (b) adding site dummies removes most of the bias, (c) residual bias persists through chance imbalance in small sites. Then quantify: run 500 simulations and histogram the adjusted-coefficient estimates — this is “regression adjustment as a bias-reducer, not a bias-eraser.”
C2 (categorical × 0.3 pandas). Take the wide expression table from 0.3 Exercise 3, melt it long, add a fake batch label, and test batch effect per gene: fit value ~ batch for each of the 5 genes with a loop of formulas. Which genes show batch effects at the joint-F level? Then write the two-sentence methods paragraph you’d put in a paper — this pattern (long-format + per-gene regression + joint F) is the skeleton of differential-expression pipelines like the T2 workflow in Part 12.

title: 2.6 Categorical Predictors
text:
7. Summary

Categories enter regression as k−1 dummies against a chosen baseline; coefficients are offsets from it.
All dummies + intercept = the trap (singular design); C() and drop_first=True are the habits.
Baseline choice changes the printed contrasts, never the fit; pick the baseline your audience reasons in.
Numeric coding of nominal labels fabricates order and spacing — a model, not a convenience.
One-way ANOVA is this page’s regression with a single categorical predictor; the machinery mixes freely with numeric predictors.
Numeric + categorical with a shared slope assumes parallel effects — the assumption 2.7 Interaction terms exists to interrogate.

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text: So far every model assumed additive effects: each predictor shifts y by a fixed amount regardless of the others. An interaction lets the effect of one predictor depend on another — the model’s most commonly forgotten question, and the difference between “drug works” and “drug works in women under 60.”

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
1. Basic Concept
Add a product column:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3\, x_1 x_2 + \varepsilon\]
Now the effect of \(x_1\) is \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 x_2\) — a function of \(x_2\), not a number. If \(\beta_3 \ne 0\), the lines/planes tilt against each other; there is no single “effect of \(x_1\)” to report.






Read the coefficients directly: male slope = dose = 0.80; female slope = dose + dose:female = 0.80 − 0.12 = 0.68; the female level offset at dose 0 = female = −1.0.
Continuous × continuous — the effect of one variable changes linearly with the other:

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
2. Concept Questions

In yield ~ temp * conc, what exactly does the conc coefficient mean now? Why is it “the effect of conc at temp = 0”?
Your interaction p-value is 0.4 but a main effect’s p-value is 0.001. May you drop the interaction and keep the main effect? May you drop the non-significant main effect and keep a significant interaction?
Interaction vs correlation between predictors (2.5 collinearity) — what’s the difference in what each breaks?
The model says the drug×sex interaction is 0.5 (p = 0.01). A headline says “drug works better in women.” What extra number does the headline need?
Why do people center variables before forming interactions, and what changes vs stays the same?



Answers


With the product term present, the conc effect is \(\beta_{conc} + \beta_{temp:conc}\,\text{temp}\) — it has no single value; by the algebra of “hold everything else fixed,” the printed \(\beta_{conc}\) is the conc effect evaluated at temp = 0. Since temp = 0 may be outside the data, that number can be meaningless — center temp and it becomes “at average temp.”
Drop the interaction: yes (back to the additive model — standard hierarchy downward is fine after a null result). Drop a main effect while keeping its interaction: no — the hierarchy principle: an interaction contains the main effects, and removing them forces the model through artificial constraints (e.g., zero effect at the other variable’s zero) that bias everything.
Collinearity is about redundant information (identifying coefficients; inflates SEs); interaction is about structure (whether effects multiply/moderate each other). Two collinear predictors can have zero interaction; two interacting predictors can be perfectly independent. Fixing one never fixes the other.
The two slopes (or the two marginal effects at meaningful values) with CIs: “slope in women = a (b to c), in men = d (e to f)” — the interaction coefficient alone doesn’t say which group is bigger, and “better” needs the scale (also: a significant interaction can mean “less bad in men”!).
Centering (subtracting means) makes main-effect coefficients interpretable at typical values of the moderator and reduces the correlation between the product column and its ingredients (numerical conditioning). It does not change fitted values, R², the interaction coefficient, or its test (with raw quadratic terms, tiny rounding aside).

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Simulate a cross-over interaction: treatment helps at low severity, harms at high severity (y = 10 + 1.0·sev − 0.8·trt + 0.2·sev·trt + noise). Fit the interaction model; compute the treatment effect at severity 2, 5, 8 with CIs (delta-method-free: refit with re-centered severity); find the severity where the effect crosses zero and verify by plotting both lines.


Solution







Re-centering the moderator converts “effect at severity s” into a main effect with proper SE and CI — no delta method needed. The cross-over point (≈ 4 here) is where the treatment recommendation flips; interactions are how subgroup medicine becomes honest instead of a fishing expedition.

Exercise 2. Test the parallel-slopes assumption from 2.6 Exercise 3 properly: fit the age × tissue model on that cohort, use anova_lm to compare against the additive model, and draw the fitted age-lines per tissue on one plot. Then write the sentence the additive model would have printed if the interaction were real but ignored — what goes wrong in it?


Solution







The pooled slope is a precision-weighted average of different per-group slopes; an “age effect” headline from the additive model would be an artifact of group composition — Simpson-adjacent, and invisible without the interaction test.

Exercise 3. Continuous × continuous as a surface: fit yield ~ temp * conc (data regenerated below), then plot the marginal effect of conc (with 95% CI) as a function of temp using the re-centering trick at a grid of temperatures. At which temperatures is conc’s effect significantly positive? This “moderated effect plot” is the professional alternative to staring at coefficient tables.


Solution







The effect grows linearly with temp (that IS the interaction) and its CI clears zero everywhere here — but the plot is what a collaborator can read: “the concentration benefit ranges from ~1.5 at 10° to ~3 at 40°.” Tables report; plots convince.

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Hierarchy principle: keep main effects whenever their interaction is present (dropping them constrains effects at the origin and biases estimates). Adding a non-significant interaction downward (simplifying) is fine; building interaction-only models is not.
“No significant interaction” ≠ “no interaction” — power for interactions is famously low (you’re estimating a difference of slopes); absence of evidence again (1.4). Check what effect size the CI rules out.
Interpretability of main effects dies with the interaction — the printed β̂_x is the effect at moderator = 0, often outside data. Center, or report effects at grid values (Exercise 1/3 pattern).
Polynomial terms are self-interactions: x² is “x interacting with x” (curvature), x³ more so — everything on this page (centering, hierarchy, interpretation at values) applies to 2.8.
Multiplicative hypotheses hide in logs: log(y) ~ x * g interactions are ratios of ratios — a significant interaction can mean “proportional effect differs,” which looks different back on the raw scale.
Multiple interactions multiply the search space — each added product is another test (Part 12’s problem in miniature); pre-specify the interactions theory predicts rather than sweeping all pairs.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated subgroup analysis has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Two subgroup fits test slopes informally and underpowered: comparing two p-values (“significant here, not there”) is not an interaction test — differences of significant/non-significant are themselves noisy. Fix: one model with dose * sex, interaction tested once with full power.
dose + dose:sex violates hierarchy: no sex main effect forces both groups’ lines through the same intercept — a strong, unjustified constraint that biases the interaction estimate itself.
“+1.0 for everyone” contradicts the model being fit: with an interaction, the dose effect is slope + interaction×sex — the sentence is only true for sex = 0 (and the printed main effect is at sex = 0 by construction).

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show algebraically that centering both predictors before forming the product leaves the fitted values, R², and the interaction coefficient unchanged, and derive exactly what happens to the main-effect coefficients. Then state the one situation in which centering changes conclusions.


Hint

Write \(x_1 = \tilde x_1 + m_1\) (m = mean), expand the product term, and match coefficients between parameterizations.



Solution

With \(x_1 = \tilde x_1 + m_1\), \(x_2 = \tilde x_2 + m_2\): \(x_1x_2 = \tilde x_1\tilde x_2 + m_2\tilde x_1 + m_1\tilde x_2 + m_1m_2\). Substituting and regrouping shows the new model is a reparameterization of the same column space (each new column is a combination of old columns), so fitted values and R² are identical; the interaction coefficient is unchanged (\(\tilde\beta_{12} = \beta_{12}\)) while new mains absorb shifts: \(\tilde\beta_1 = \beta_1 + m_2\beta_{12}\) — precisely “the x₁ effect at \(x_2 = m_2\).” The SEs of the mains change (they estimate different quantities at different points). Conclusions change only when you interpret the main effects: at moderator = 0 (raw, possibly absurd) vs moderator = mean (centered, meaningful). Same model, different sentences — which is why centering is an interpretation tool, not a statistics fix.

Q2. An interaction is significant in a discovery cohort (n = 400) and you plan a confirmatory cohort (n = 400). Given that interaction power is low, design the confirmation: what is tested, what alpha, what counts as replication (same sign? CI overlap? pre-registered effect size?), and what does the “winner’s curse” of the discovery estimate imply for the expected confirmatory effect size? Demonstrate the winner’s curse by simulation.


Solution







Design: (1) test the same, pre-registered interaction in the confirmation cohort at one-sided α = 0.05 in the pre-stated direction; (2) replication = significant and same sign, ideally with effect size inside the discovery CI’s plausible range; CI overlap alone is far too weak (overlapping CIs are consistent with significant differences); (3) the winner’s curse: conditional on being selected for p < 0.05 under the null, the discovery estimate averages ~1 SE in magnitude (simulation above: false hits with mean |β̂| ≈ 0.1 SD against truth 0) — so shrink expectations: the confirmatory estimate will typically be smaller than the discovery headline even when real. Report both cohorts’ estimates side by side, never the discovery estimate alone as “the effect.”

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (interaction × 2.6 Categorical × 1.2 Simpson). Construct data where: pooled slope is positive, every group’s slope is negative, and the group×x interaction is significant. This is Simpson’s paradox with heterogeneous slopes — show the three nested models (pooled, dummies, dummies×x) and write which model each of three stakeholders (hospital administrator, per-site clinician, meta-analyst) should read.
C2 (interaction × 4.6 Tuning preview). Generate data with a true interaction and compare the out-of-sample performance of (a) the additive model, (b) the correctly specified interaction model, (c) the all-pairs-interactions model (x1:x2, x1:x3, x2:x3, x1:x2:x3 with 4 predictors), across n = 40, 100, 400. Which model wins at each n, and what does this tell you about interaction hunting as a function of sample size — before you ever look at a p-value?

title: 2.7 Interaction Terms
text:
7. Summary

An interaction makes an effect a function: β₃ ≠ 0 means “the effect of x₁ depends on x₂.”
Report effects at meaningful moderator values (re-center and read main effects) — never the raw table alone.
Hierarchy principle: keep main effects with their interaction; simplify downward only.
Subgroup p-value comparisons are not interaction tests; one product term, tested once, has the power.
Centering changes interpretation, never fit; polynomial curvature is interaction with itself.
Interaction power is low; absence of evidence needs the CI’s effect-size statement.
Linearity itself is now the last standing structural assumption — 2.8 Nonlinear feature transformations bends the line without leaving the linear-model world.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text: Linear models fit straight lines in their parameters — but the features can be any transform of x you like: polynomials, logs, splines, binned indicators. This buys curvature inside the same least-squares machinery, at the price of the same old dangers (overfitting, extrapolation) in sharper form.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
1. Basic Concept
“Linear” in \(X\beta\) refers to the coefficients. Replace \(x\) by any derived columns and the model stays linear-in-parameters:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \varepsilon \qquad \text{or} \qquad \log y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \log x + \varepsilon\]
Polynomial regression of degree d is just OLS on the design matrix \([1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^d]\):






Degree 2 wins here because the truth is quadratic. Degree 9 chases noise — same lesson the U-curve will make quantitative in 4.1.
Log transforms linearize power laws and stabilize multiplicative noise (0.4):






Binning (step features) is the crudest nonlinearity — cut x into ranges, dummy them (2.6):

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is polynomial regression still a “linear model”? What precisely is linear?
Degree 12 polynomial through 60 points: fitted values look perfect, predictions on new data are wild. Name the two quantities whose divergence you are witnessing.
Your y spans decades of magnitude with constant relative error. Which transform, and what does the slope mean if you regress \(\log_{10} y\) on \(\log_{10} x\)?
Extrapolation danger: compare a linear fit and a degree-9 polynomial fit extended 20% beyond the data. Which fails more catastrophically, and why — what does the polynomial do outside the data’s support?
log(y) model gives RMSE(log-scale) = 0.2. A colleague multiplies by exp to report “RMSE = 1.22” on the raw scale. What did they actually compute, and what is the right comparison?



Answers


Linear in the coefficients \(\beta\): the model is \(\beta^\top \phi(x)\) for basis functions \(\phi\) (powers, logs of x — transforms of features, not of parameters). Estimation is still OLS on a design matrix.
In-sample error (falls as degree rises — more flexibility always fits training better) vs out-of-sample error (rises once curvature fits noise). The gap is overfitting; Part 4 measures it, Part 5 penalizes it.
log–log (power-law) transform; slope = the power exponent (y ∝ x^slope), intercept gives the multiplicative prefactor. Only after confirming constant relative scatter — the log makes multiplicative errors additive (0.4 Q2).
The polynomial. A line continues its slope; a degree-9 fit’s leading coefficient (estimated from noise) dominates outside the data, swinging to ±astronomical values. Polynomials are global basis functions — a wiggle fitted inside must resolve into a violent curve outside. Local bases (splines, Part 6) behave far better.
exp(0.2) = 1.22 is a median-level multiplicative miss (the error of a typical log-residual), not an RMSE in y-units — RMSE is not transform-invertible (Jensen: E[y − ŷ] ≠ exp(E[log-residual])). The honest comparison back-transforms predictions (accepting median-level bias, or smearing-correcting) and computes RMSE on the raw scale.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the quadratic-truth data below, fit degrees 1–7 and collect training MSE and test MSE (fresh points from the same process). Plot both against degree. Mark the argmin of test MSE, then repeat the whole experiment with n = 300 — how does the curve’s shape change and what does that tell you about “more data vs simpler model”?


Solution







At n = 30 the test curve is jagged — degree choice is nearly a coin flip among low degrees. At n = 300 the minimum sharpens around the true degree 2 and high degrees hurt less (more data tames the variance term). Data volume substitutes for model restraint — the trade 4.4 will formalize.

Exercise 2. Linearize a real-ish process: enzyme velocity follows \(v = \frac{V_{max} s}{K_m + s}\) (Michaelis–Menten) with \(V_{max} = 2\), \(K_m = 0.4\). Fit (a) a direct polynomial of degree 2 on (s, v), and (b) the classic Lineweaver–Burk linearization (\(1/v\) vs \(1/s\), whose slope = \(K_m/V_{max}\), intercept = \(1/V_{max}\)) using OLS. Recover \(V_{max}\) and \(K_m\) from each. Which recovers the truth better under noise, and what famous statistical vice does Lineweaver–Burk have?


Solution







The reciprocal transform converts multiplicative-ish errors into heteroscedastic ones and hands all the leverage to the smallest s — the few noisiest points steer the line. The polynomial dodges that trap but estimates \(V_{max}\) as a plateau asymptote. Modern practice: fit the nonlinear model directly with least squares (Part 6 territory) — linearizations are history’s workaround, not a virtue.

Exercise 3. Build poly_cv(x, y, max_degree, k=5) returning mean CV MSE per degree using a Pipeline(StandardScaler-with-PolynomialFeatures, LinearRegression) — scaling before polynomial expansion to keep raw powers numerically sane. Run it on data with a cubic truth; report the chosen degree and the CV curve. Then explain why the pipeline (transform inside each fold) matters — connect to the leakage rule of 0.5.


Solution







If you scaled/expanded before splitting, each fold’s training statistics (means, SDs) leak test-fold information into training — mild here, systematic everywhere. The pipeline runs the transform per-fold inside cross_val_score, guaranteeing the validation fold is touched only by the fitted-for-that-fold transform. The 0.5 rule — “fit preprocessing inside the training fold” — generalizes to every transformer you will ever use.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Global vs local bases: polynomial features are global — every observation informs every coefficient, so one leverage point reshapes the whole curve. Splines/step functions are local (Part 6 covers them properly; the binned drill is a preview).
Numerical conditioning: raw powers of x (say x ∈ [0, 1000], degree 6) make columns nearly collinear and ill-conditioned — coefficients become garbage even when predictions look fine. Standardize x first, or use orthogonal polynomials (np.polynomial.legendre.legvander, or sklearn’s scaled pipeline).
The polynomial tail kills: never report extrapolated polynomial predictions; if you must extrapolate, extrapolate the physics (a fitted asymptote, a log-linearized regime), not the polynomial.
Transforming y changes the error model: log y regression minimizes log-scale squared error — predictions are medians on the raw scale and need smearing if means are wanted; RMSE comparisons across scales are meaningless (2.4).
Binning throws away information and induces boundary artifacts; it’s a quick diagnostic (is there structure?) rather than an endpoint. Smooth bases or splines dominate it for inference and prediction alike.
Degree choice is a hyperparameter — choosing it by looking at the same data you report performance on is the classic optimism; route the choice through CV now, formally in 4.6.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated curve-fit has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Raw powers of x up to 100⁸ — the design matrix has condition number ~10¹⁶; coefficients are numerically meaningless (look at their wild magnitudes). Fix: standardize x before expanding (or orthogonal polynomials).
Extrapolating a degree-8 fit to x = 500 (5× beyond data): the leading noise-driven coefficient explodes — “predictions” of ±billions. Fix: police the range; extrapolate with theory-bounded models only.
RMSEs on different scales (y vs log y) — not comparable (2.4). Fix: back-transform log predictions and compare on one scale.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Show that adding any column \(g(x)\) to a linear model’s design matrix can only decrease training RSS, and quantify the minimum decrease in terms of the residual regression: if \(g\)’s component orthogonal to the current columns explains RSS reduction \(\Delta\), write the updated fit. Use this to explain why degree-9 training RSS < degree-2 training RSS even when truth is quadratic, and what determines whether the test RSS follows.


Hint

Projection geometry from 2.4 Q1: OLS projects y onto the column space; a bigger space projects further.



Solution

OLS fit = orthogonal projection of y onto span(columns). Adding a column enlarges the span, and projections onto supersets are never worse: new RSS = old RSS − ‖proj of y onto g⊥(old columns)‖² = old RSS − Δ, with Δ ≥ 0. For the noise-only extra powers, Δ = the squared length of the chance alignment of the noise with those directions — positive in every sample, growing with the number of added columns. Test RSS follows only if the true f has a component in the new directions that outweighs the variance those directions import (each extra coefficient costs ~σ²·(df) of variance in predictions — the arithmetic 4.4 makes explicit). In-sample improvement is therefore guaranteed, meaningful only if structural.

Q2. You must model \(y = f(x)\) where f is believed smooth and you have n = 40 points. Compare, in one experiment, (a) global polynomial degree chosen by CV, (b) 10-bin step function, (c) the “transformed linear” model \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 \sin(x)\) when the truth is \(3\sin(x)\). Report test MSEs and state the general lesson about basis choice informed by mechanism vs generic flexible bases.


Solution







The mechanistic two-column model usually wins outright (right basis, 3 parameters); CV-polynomials get close with 5–8 parameters; steps are worst (boundary steps, step noise). Lesson: a small basis derived from how the system works beats generic flexibility at small n — save the flexible machinery for when mechanism is unknown and n is large.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (transforms × 2.10 Assumptions preview). Generate multiplicative-noise data (\(y = 2x\,e^{\varepsilon}\)). Fit (a) y ~ x, (b) log y ~ log x, and diagnose each with residuals-vs-fitted and QQ plots. State which assumption each fit violates and how the diagnostic revealed it — then connect the funnel and the skewed residuals to 0.4 Q2’s log-scale advice.
C2 (transforms × 4.1 Generalization preview). Using the degree-sweep experiment from Exercise 1, decompose test MSE at each degree into bias² and variance by simulating 300 training sets (evaluate each degree’s fitted curve on a fixed grid, average across training sets). Plot the three curves (bias², variance, total) against degree. You have built the bias–variance picture before the theory page — bring the plot to 4.4 and check it against the decomposition there.

title: 2.8 Nonlinear Feature Transformations
text:
7. Summary

“Linear” means linear in coefficients; polynomials, logs, bins, sin — any derived columns — stay in OLS-land.
Higher degree always improves training fit and eventually wrecks test fit; degree is a hyperparameter, chosen by CV.
Log transforms linearize power laws (slope = exponent) and convert multiplicative noise to additive; back-transform carefully (medians, not means).
Polynomials are global bases: numerically fragile raw, catastrophic in extrapolation; standardize before expanding.
Transforming y changes the error model and the meaning of every metric; compare models on one scale.
Mechanism-informed small bases beat generic flexible bases at small n.
The residual from a transformed fit must still be inspected — the full diagnostic toolkit is next: 2.10 Regression assumptions, after a nonparametric detour in 2.9 KNN regression.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text: Simple linear regression fits a straight line \(\hat{y} = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 x\) by least squares. It is the reference point for every model in this course: transparent, closed-form, and already rich enough to demonstrate estimation, uncertainty, and mis-use.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
Least squares chooses coefficients minimizing the residual sum of squares \(\text{RSS} = \sum_i (y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i)^2\). Minimizing in each parameter (set derivatives to zero) gives the closed forms:
\[\hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = r\,\frac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad \hat{\beta}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}\]
The slope is the correlation rescaled into y-units per x-unit (1.2); the line always passes through \((\bar x, \bar y)\).












Reading the coefficients. \(\hat\beta_1\): predicted change in \(y\) per one-unit increase in \(x\). \(\hat\beta_0\): prediction at \(x = 0\) — meaningful only if 0 is in (or near) the data’s range; otherwise it is an extrapolated anchor, not a “baseline effect.”

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why does the least-squares line always pass through \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\)?
Data in x = Fahrenheit, y = Celsius is fit with slope \(\hat\beta_1\). Refit in x = Kelvin. What happens to the slope and intercept?
Your slope is 4.2 with r = 0.3. What is \(s_y / s_x\) telling you here, and would you call this a “strong” effect?
Two students fit the same data; one forgets the intercept term (forces \(\hat\beta_0 = 0\)). Whose slope changes, and in which direction is it biased if \(\bar y\) and \(\bar x\) are both positive?
What is the RSS of the perfect-intercept model (\(\hat\beta_1 = 0\))? (Connects to 2.1 Q1.)



Answers


\(\hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x\) rearranges to \(\bar y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \bar x\) — a direct consequence of the first-order condition in \(\beta_0\) (residuals sum to zero).
Kelvin = Fahrenheit-scaled shift: \(x_K = (x_F + 459.67) \times \frac{5}{9}\). Slope rescales by the x-unit factor: \(\hat\beta_1^{(K)} = \hat\beta_1^{(F)} \cdot \frac{9}{5}\); intercept absorbs the shift via the point \((\bar x, \bar y)\). Slope is unit-sensitive; correlation r is not.
\(s_y/s_x = 4.2/0.3 = 14\) — the slope is large only because y varies 14× more than x. “Strong” is about r (or standardized slope), not \(\hat\beta_1\) alone: r = 0.3 is a weak linear signal with a steep unit conversion. Always report effect in context: 4.2 y-units per x-unit with uncertainty.
Without an intercept, \(\hat\beta_1\) must do double duty (slope + level), and the first-order condition \(\sum r_i = 0\) is lost. With positive \(\bar x, \bar y\), the no-intercept slope is biased upward — it’s pulled toward \(y/x\) ratios rather than the local slope. Force an intercept unless a theory demands the line pass through the origin (and then still check).
\(\text{RSS} = \sum(y_i - \bar y)^2 = \text{TSS}\) — the mean-model. Every slope model is judged by how much it shrinks this number; that comparison becomes \(R^2\) in 2.4.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Compute the least-squares slope and intercept from scratch (sums only, no polyfit/sklearn) for the dataset below, then verify against np.polyfit. Report RSS and compare it to the TSS of the intercept-only model.


Solution







RSS ≪ TSS here: the line explains most of the variation. That ratio — computed again with proper degrees of freedom — becomes \(R^2\) and \(R^2_{\text{adj}}\) in 2.4.

Exercise 2. Regression to the mean, experienced: simulate 200 parents’ heights and children’s heights as child = 0.7*parent + 68 + noise (units: inches). Fit child ~ parent. Report the slope and predicted child height for a parent at 62 in and at 76 in. Explain — in one sentence each — why the predictions sit closer to the population mean than the inputs, and why this is a statistical fact and not a biological force.


Solution







Predictions are pulled toward \(\bar y\) because slope < 1: a parent 4 in below the mean is predicted only ~2.8 in below-average child. The mechanism is pure statistics — the parent’s deviation partially reflects parent-side luck (noise), which doesn’t repeat in the child. Any noisy pair with \(|\rho| < 1\) regresses to the mean; misreading it as causal “correction” is the classic historical error (Galton’s own).

Exercise 3. Prediction interval preview by simulation: fit the line on n = 40 points (\(\sigma = 2\) known truth), then simulate the empirical distribution of predictions at x = 5 over 2,000 re-generated training sets. Report the SD of predictions and compare it to (a) the SD of a single new observation at x = 5 (≈ σ) and (b) the SE of the mean response. Which interval is wider — confidence or prediction — and why?


Solution







The fitted mean response at x = 5 is much more stable than any individual point: individual outcomes add irreducible σ on top of the mean’s uncertainty. Hence the prediction interval (for a new y) is always wider than the confidence interval (for the mean) — quantified properly in 2.3–2.4.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

np.polyfit returns highest-degree first ([slope, intercept] for deg 1) — reversing them is a top silent bug. np.polyval([b1, b0], x_new) matches.
sklearn wants 2-D X: model.fit(x, y) with 1-D x raises — x.reshape(-1, 1) or x[:, None] (0.2 broadcasting).
Extrapolation — the line continues with full confidence beyond the data; the only protection is range-checking (2.1).
Outliers have leverage proportional to \((x - \bar x)^2\) — far-in-x points can rotate the whole line (Anscombe III in 1.2); check the fit with and without suspects.
Slope ≠ effect without design: in observational data \(\hat\beta_1\) is an association per unit x; confounding can give any sign (2.5, 2.6).
Correlation of residuals is the real assumption — independence, not normality, is what makes the classic SEs valid; time-order or cluster structure breaks it quietly (2.10).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated fit-and-report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


polyfit order reversed: it returns [highest-degree, ..., constant], so b0 here is the slope and b1 the intercept — every printed label lies. Fix: b1, b0 = np.polyfit(...) or unpack with names.
Reversed-coefficient prediction then residuals: garbage in, garbage out; also the residual-mean check only works when the intercept is present (it should be ≈ 0 numerically). Fix names, then check.
Self-congratulatory metric: corr(fitted, x) is always ≈ ±1 by construction — it measures the line’s steepness, not fit quality. Fix: compare against y (residual-based: RSS vs TSS, or corr(ŷ, y)).

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove that regressing standardized $y^* $ on standardized \(x^*\) yields slope = r and intercept = 0, and derive from it the identity \(\hat\beta_1 = r\, s_y / s_x\). Why does this make the slope unit-sensitive while r is not?


Hint

Standardized variables have mean 0, variance 1; apply the closed-form slope.



Solution

With \(x^* = (x-\bar x)/s_x\), \(y^* = (y - \bar y)/s_y\): slope \(= \frac{\sum x_i^* y_i^*}{\sum x_i^{*2}} = \frac{(n-1)\,\text{cov}(x^*,y^*)}{(n-1)\,\text{var}(x^*)} = r\) (both variances are 1); intercept \(= \bar y^* - r\bar x^* = 0\). Rescaling \(y^* \to y\) multiplies the slope by \(s_y\); rescaling \(x^* \to x\) divides it by \(s_x\) — giving \(\hat\beta_1 = r s_y/s_x\). So \(\hat\beta_1\) mixes a dimensionless association strength (r) with a unit conversion (\(s_y/s_x\)): change x to centimeters and the slope divides by 2.54 with no change in reality. This is why cross-study comparisons report standardized coefficients or r, and why “bigger slope = stronger effect” is meaningless across unit systems.

Q2. Under what exact conditions does the least-squares slope equal the causal effect of x on y? Use a simulation where x is correlated with an unobserved driver of y to show \(\hat\beta_1\) ≠ true effect, and connect the size of the gap to the confounder’s correlation with x and y.


Solution

Causal equality requires no confounding: \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon \mid x] = 0\) — the error (which contains all other causes) uncorrelated with x; in a randomized experiment this holds by design, in observational data it’s an assumption. Simulation:






The naive slope overshoots: part of z’s influence on y rides in through corr(x, z). First-order intuition: \(\hat\beta_1 \approx \text{true} + \beta_z \cdot \delta\) where δ is the x–confounder association. The general cure is adjusting for measured confounders (2.5, 2.6); unmeasured ones limit every observational claim.

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (SLR × 1.5 Resampling). Bootstrap the slope of the Exercise 1 dataset (5,000 resamples) and compare the bootstrap SD of \(\hat\beta_1\) to the formula-based SE from 2.3. Now inject one high-leverage outlier (x = 40, y = 10) and redo both. Which SE detects the fragility first, and what does this say about formula-SE trust on real data?
C2 (SLR × 0.3 pandas). Load the cohort-style frame: 4 groups with different slopes on a shared x. Fit (a) one pooled line, (b) separate lines per group via groupby. Under what parameter constellation does the pooled slope equal a (weighted) average of group slopes, and when can its sign contradict all of them? (This is Simpson’s paradox armed with slopes — resolved with dummies in 2.6.)

title: 2.2 Simple Linear Regression
text:
7. Summary

Least squares has closed forms; the line passes through \((\bar x, \bar y)\); slope = \(r\,s_y/s_x\).
np.polyfit orders coefficients highest-power-first; sklearn wants 2-D X — mechanical details that produce silent bugs.
Intercept = prediction at x = 0: interpret only when 0 is in-range.
Slope is unit-sensitive, r is not; neither is causal without design or adjustment.
Regression to the mean follows from any \(|r| < 1\) — statistical, not substantive.
Confidence interval (mean response) is always narrower than prediction interval (new point): irreducible σ sits on top.
A line is a claim; next page asks how precisely the data pins that claim down: 2.3 Accuracy of the coefficients.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text: A slope estimate is a random variable — a different sample gives a different line. This page quantifies how much it moves: standard errors, t-tests on coefficients, and confidence intervals. This is the inference layer that separates “there’s a slope” from “we know the slope to ±0.2.”

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
1. Basic Concept
Under the model \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\) with homoscedastic, independent errors, the slope estimator has standard error
\[\text{SE}(\hat{\beta}_1) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}}{\sqrt{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2}} = \frac{\hat\sigma}{s_x\sqrt{n}} \qquad\text{where } \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\text{RSS}}{n - 2}\]
Three levers, all visible in the formula: more noise (σ) widens; more spread in x (\(s_x\)) narrows; more points (\(\sqrt n\)) narrows. The coefficient’s t-statistic and CI follow the universal pattern from 1.4:
\[t = \frac{\hat\beta_1}{\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)}, \qquad \hat\beta_1 \pm t_{0.975,\,n-2}\,\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1)\]






Same information, human-readable — and the residual-based estimate of σ:






Verify the formula by brute force — the SE is just the SD of the estimator across hypothetical samples:

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
2. Concept Questions

Two datasets have identical σ and n, but dataset A’s x spans 0–100 and B’s spans 0–1. Which has the more precise slope, and which term of the SE formula says so?
What exactly is \(H_0\) when P>|t| for a slope is 0.03? And what is not being tested?
Why do we divide RSS by \(n-2\) (not \(n\)) to estimate σ²?
Your 95% CI for a slope is (0.02, 0.11). A reviewer says “the effect is tiny.” What’s the correct reply?
If you double all y values, what happens to \(\hat\beta_1\), its SE, its t-statistic, and its p-value?



Answers


A — via \(s_x\) (x-spread) in the denominator: the same noise, stretched over a wider x-range, is harder to confuse with a slope. Note it is the spread, not the range per se — a single far point adds range without usable spread (and adds leverage instead).
\(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) — “no linear relationship with this predictor, in this model,” tested with data this size. Not tested: the effect’s practical importance (0.03 doesn’t mean “large”), causality, or the effect conditional on predictors not in the model.
Two parameters (\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)) were fitted from the same residuals, consuming 2 degrees of freedom; residuals from a fitted line are systematically smaller than true ε. Dividing by \(n - p - 1\) (here p = 1) corrects the optimism — the same logic as \(n-1\) for a variance (1.1).
“Statistically significant but small, and the estimate is 0.02–0.11 y-units per unit x.” Significance ≠ importance; the CI is the effect-size statement — argue importance against the interval’s values, not its exclusion of zero.
\(\hat\beta_1\) and SE double (both scale with y’s units) → t and p unchanged. Slope SEs live in y-units: 2× the outcome units, 2× the uncertainty — but the same evidence. (This scale-invariance of t is why p-values don’t answer “is the effect big.”)

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. For the data below, compute SE(β̂₁) by hand from the formula \(\hat\sigma / s_x\sqrt n\) (using residuals for σ̂), then match it against model.bse[1]. Construct the 95% CI manually and compare with conf_int().


Solution







Identical to 3 decimals. The formula’s three levers are now concrete: σ̂ from residuals, spread from \(s_x\), and \(\sqrt n\). (Column name “x1” is statsmodels’ generic name when X is a bare array.)

Exercise 2. Show empirically that a wider x-range buys precision for free: fix σ = 3, n = 30, true slope 0.5; compare the empirical SD of β̂₁ over 3,000 simulations when x ~ U(0, 1) vs x ~ U(0, 10). Verify the ratio matches the theory ratio \(s_{x,B}/s_{x,A}\).


Solution







A 10× wider design makes the slope estimate ~10× more precise at the same cost per observation. This is the experimental-design lever: spread your inputs (or your doses, or your temperatures) before you buy more replicates.

Exercise 3. An experimenter runs the regression below and reports: “slope p = 0.31, so x has no effect; but the R² is 0.4, so the model is strong.” Reconcile the two statements. Then demonstrate the resolution: simulate data where x has zero linear effect but determines the variance of y, and show what p-value and R² each report.


Solution

The two statements can coexist: R² measures explained variance (any source — including x’s effect on spread), while the slope p-value tests a mean-shift of y per unit x. x can move the distribution strongly (its spread) with zero mean shift:






Both statements are “right” and answer different questions — the experimenter’s sentence glued them together. The fix is reporting what was tested: for variance effects, model the spread explicitly (heteroscedastic models, GLMs 3.6), not the mean.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Formula SEs rest on all four classical assumptions (linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, rough normality for the t reference). Heteroscedasticity or correlated errors invalidate the SEs even when the slope estimate stays unbiased — the point estimate and its uncertainty fail independently (2.10).
Heteroscedasticity-robust (HC) SEs are one line in statsmodels — fit(cov_type="HC3") — and are a sensible default for observational cross-sectional data.
Multiple predictors change the SE story: \(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)\) now depends on collinearity — the variance inflation factor (2.5); a coefficient can be noisy because its partners are redundant, not because n is small.
The intercept’s SE is usually the largest (it lives at the edge, \(x = 0\)): don’t be alarmed, and don’t interpret its p-value as a test of “does the model work.”
p = 0.049 vs 0.051 — no meaningful boundary; report effects with CIs and treat thresholds as conventions (1.4).
statsmodels column names: bare arrays give generic x1, x2...; use DataFrames or formulas (smf.ols) for self-documenting output.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated inference report has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Intercept p-value misread: it tests whether the line’s value at x = 0 differs from 0 — usually meaningless (x = 0 outside data) and never a verdict on the model.
p ≠ effect size: with n = 25 and σ = 3 this p-value coexists with a CI like (0.1, 1.5) — potentially important or trivial. Report β̂ ± CI.
