z instead of t: at n − 2 = 23 df the t-critical value is 2.069, not 1.96 — small samples widen; use conf_int() (or t-quantile) so the interval is honest.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive \(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \hat\sigma / \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}\) in two steps: (a) write \(\hat\beta_1\) as a weighted sum of the \(y_i\) with weights \(w_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}\), and (b) apply the independent-errors variance rule from 1.3. Which property of the weights (\(\sum w_i = 0\)) makes β̂₀ drop out?


Hint

\(\hat\beta_1 = \sum w_i y_i\) exactly; variances add for independent errors and intercept enters only through the centered cross-product.



Solution


\(\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x) y_i}{S_{xx}}\) (the \(-\bar y\) term vanishes since \(\sum (x_i - \bar x) = 0\)) — a linear combination \(\sum w_i y_i\) with \(w_i = (x_i - \bar x)/S_{xx}\). (b) With independent homoscedastic errors: \(\text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \sum w_i^2 \sigma^2 = \sigma^2 \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}\). The same centering (\(\sum w_i = 0\)) makes \(\hat\beta_1\)’s sampling distribution independent of where β₀ sits — the two estimates’ covariance is zero under normality (basis of independent slope/intercept CIs). This is the seed of the full covariance matrix \(\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}\) for multiple regression (2.5).


Q2. Estimate the sampling distribution of β̂₁ by bootstrap for the Exercise 1 data and compare: (a) bootstrap SD vs formula SE, (b) bootstrap percentile CI vs t-CI. Now regenerate the data with heteroscedastic noise (\(\sigma \propto x\)) and repeat. Which comparison breaks, and what is the bootstrap version measuring that the formula no longer estimates?


Solution







Homoscedastic: the two agree (formula valid). Heteroscedastic: they diverge — the formula assumes one σ, the bootstrap re-encounters the actual error structure in the resamples, so it estimates the real sampling variability. The bootstrap is the general-purpose audit of any formula SE; when they disagree, trust the bootstrap and fix the assumptions (robust SEs or a GLM).

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (coefficient accuracy × 0.5 Data splitting). Fit the same SLR on 200 different 80/20 splits; collect slope estimates and their formula SEs each time. Plot SE(slope) against the x-spread of the training split. What relationship emerges, how does it connect to the SE formula, and why does stratifying or blocking matter more for slope stability than for intercept stability?
C2 (coefficient accuracy × 2.5 Multiple regression preview). Generate \(y = 2x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2 + \varepsilon\) with \(x_2 = 0.95 x_1 + \text{noise}\) (collinear partners). Compare the SE of the \(x_1\) coefficient in (a) the single-predictor model and (b) the two-predictor model. Quantify the inflation and explain it as redundancy: the data cannot tell the two “explanations” apart, so uncertainty per coefficient explodes — the multicollinearity story of 2.5.

title: 2.3 Accuracy of the Coefficients
text:
7. Summary

\(\text{SE}(\hat\beta_1) = \hat\sigma/(s_x\sqrt n)\): less noise, wider x-spread, more n — tighter slopes.
t = β̂/SE against \(H_0{:}\,\beta = 0\); the CI, not the p-value, is the effect-size statement.
σ̂ uses \(n - p - 1\) df: fitted parameters consumed the residual information.
t-tests are scale-invariant (double y → double β̂, SE; same t) — they measure evidence, not size.
Formula SEs assume linearity, independence, homoscedasticity; robust SEs and the bootstrap are the practical audits.
Wide x-design is the cheapest precision you will ever buy.
One coefficient is one part of the model; next page scores the whole fit: 2.4 Accuracy of the full model.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text: You now own five classifiers (logistic, LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes, KNN). Choosing between them is where careless pipelines go to lie to themselves: comparing on one split, one metric, or — worst — the metric that was also used to tune. This page builds the honest comparison protocol: same folds, paired tests, calibration checks, and decision-aware selection.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
1. Basic Concept
Three principles of fair comparison:

Same folds, paired evaluation — models see identical train/test partitions; differences are then within-fold, far less noisy than independent estimates.
Metrics match the decision — AUC/AP for ranking, calibration for probabilities, operating-point metrics for budgets (3.1, 3.1.5).
Uncertainty on differences, not just points — a 0.01 AUC gap between two models on one split is noise until tested.

The canonical setup, all five models on identical CV folds:






Paired comparison — the same fold’s differences, tested. For two models’ predictions on the same test rows, McNemar’s test asks whether the disagreement pattern is asymmetric:






Calibration — do predicted probabilities mean what they say? The reliability diagram:

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a paired comparison (same folds) so much more powerful than comparing two independent 5-fold means?
Two models have AUC 0.81 and 0.83. List, in order, the three facts you need before believing the second is better.
What does a model above the diagonal in a reliability diagram (observed > predicted) indicate, and name one common pipeline step that causes systematic miscalibration.
Why can Naive Bayes have a worse Brier score but nearly identical AUC to logistic — and when would you still ship NB?
You tuned model A’s hyperparameters by CV and want to compare against untuned model B. What does honest comparison require?



Answers


Fold-to-fold difficulty dominates variance (easy folds flatter everyone). Pairing differences out that shared noise: Var(diff) = Var(A) + Var(B) − 2Cov(A,B), and the fold-correlation makes the covariance term large — paired tests see the signal that independent-mean comparisons drown in. The same logic as paired t-tests (1.4).

Uncertainty: is 0.02 within fold/seed noise (paired fold-wise test)? (2) Same preprocessing/tuning budget for both? (3) Does the metric match the deployment question — and does the gap replicate on a held-out set or fresh data?

Observed frequency exceeds predicted probability → the model is systematically underconfident in that region. Causes: training on resampled/oversampled data (case–control sampling shifts the intercept — 3.3 C2); regularization that shrinks logits toward the base rate in the wrong direction; score warping in NB under feature correlation.
Brier scores squared-error penalties punish NB’s overconfident probabilities (3.4); AUC, being rank-based, is blind to that inflation. Ship NB when you consume rankings (top-k retrieval) and cost nothing by probability errors — its speed and small-sample stability then win.
Either tune B with the identical CV protocol (same folds/grid budget) or evaluate both with an outer CV layer untouched by tuning — nested evaluation (4.6). Comparing a tuned model’s selection-optimized number against an untuned model’s plain number conflates selection luck with model quality.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Build compare_models(models, X, y, k=5, seed=0) returning a DataFrame of mean±SD accuracy, AUC, AP plus pairwise McNemar p-values on pooled out-of-fold predictions. Run it on the five classifiers of Section 1; identify (a) the statistical leader, (b) the pair whose difference is not significant, (c) which metric(s) disagree with accuracy’s ranking.


Solution







Caveat carried forward: pooled out-of-fold predictions are not fully independent across folds for the McNemar counts (models refit per fold), but the paired structure is preserved — for publication-grade claims, repeat across outer resamples (4.3). The table + test pattern is the deliverable regardless.

Exercise 2. Calibration repair: the NB probabilities from Section 1’s reliability data are inflated. Implement a simple Platt-style fix: fit a 1-D logistic regression mapping NB’s logit-scored output to the true labels on a validation split, apply to test. Show Brier before/after and the reliability diagrams side by side. Confirm AUC is unchanged (rank-preserving map) — then state when this fix is not legitimate (which data it must not touch).


Solution







The calibration map is fit on a dedicated split that played no role in training the NB — touching the test set (or the original training set) for calibration would re-introduce optimism (0.5). AUC is invariant (monotone map); Brier collapses toward the logistic’s. This split discipline — fit, calibrate, test on three disjoint samples — is the production-grade pattern.

Exercise 3. Decision-theoretic selection: two models, fixed budget of 100 follow-ups per 5,000 screened (1% prevalence). Compute for each model the expected number of true hits in its top-100 (per 10 bootstrap resamples of the screening population), with a CI on the difference. Also compute each model’s precision@100. Which model wins the deployment question, and does it match the AUC winner?


Solution







The bootstrap CI on hits-in-top-100 is the deployment metric with uncertainty attached. If it excludes 0, the decision is made regardless of what AUC says — models with similar AUC can differ sharply in the head of the ranking, and budgets only ever buy the head.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The comparison protocol IS the result: same folds, same preprocessing (pipelines), same tuning budget, paired tests, uncertainty on differences. Deviating from any of these resets the table to anecdote.
Pooled out-of-fold predictions (Exercise 1) preserve pairing but fold-refitting leaks mild dependence across folds — fine for exploration; use repeated outer resampling for claims.
McNemar’s exact test is binomial on discordant pairs — b and c only; concordant pairs carry no comparison information. Low discordance = low power, whatever the accuracies say.
Brier vs AUC rank: fixing calibration never changes AUC (monotone maps) — which is why “we recalibrated and AUC didn’t move” is expected, not suspicious.
Multiple models ⇒ multiple comparisons: 5 models = 10 pairwise tests; control family-wise error (Bonferroni ×10) or pre-specify the primary comparison (12.3–12.4 preview).
Selection on the comparison metric: if the winner’s metric then becomes the reported performance, the number is selection-inflated — the nested-CV discipline of 4.6 applies with full force.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated “model selection” has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Model selection on the full dataset including the evaluation rows — the test set is spent tuning (0.5). Select by CV inside training only.
Training accuracy as final performance: KNN(k=1) scores 1.0 — pure memorization crowned winner. Report held-out/CV.
Single-split gap declared decisive: one split’s difference is noise (4.1); use repeated/paired CV and a McNemar-style test before naming a winner.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. The “no free lunch” caveat says no classifier dominates universally. Construct two 2-D problems — one where logistic beats KNN decisively, one where KNN beats logistic — with identical n and noise. Report both test-accuracy tables and explain each winner’s edge in terms of assumption alignment (linear boundary vs local structure). What legitimate conclusion is possible about “the best classifier” for a new problem before looking at its data?


Solution







Linear truth: logistic’s inductive bias matches the boundary — it wins. Spiral: the boundary is wildly nonlinear; KNN’s local votes trace it while logistic caps out at linear. Conclusion about a new problem, pre-data: none about which wins — only about the procedure (honest CV over a small, diverse candidate set) that finds out. Model choice is an empirical property of the problem, which is why Part 4’s machinery exists.

Q2. You must compare k=7-KNN and logistic and report a p-value for “A is better.” Walk through the construction of a paired, replicated comparison: (a) why fold-wise paired t on 5 folds is weak (df = 4, dependence), (b) how repeated 5×2-fold CV (or 20 random 80/20 replications) restores power, (c) what exactly the unit of analysis is (a replication’s difference), and (d) the multiplicity caveat if 8 models enter the same protocol. Implement (b) for two models and report the CI for the accuracy difference.


Solution








5-fold paired t has df = 4 and folds share training rows — dependence inflates the nominal Type I error (the famous Dietterich point). (b) Each replication is a fresh split: differences are far less correlated across replications; 40 replications give a stable CI. (c) The unit is the replication-level difference — treat replications as the sample. (d) Eight models ⇒ 28 pairwise CIs; multiplicity control (Bonferroni/Holm) or a pre-registered primary comparison keeps the family-wise error honest (12.3 preview).

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (comparison × 0.5 splitting × 4.3 CV). Build the full “league table” experiment: 6 classifiers × 20 repeated stratified 5-fold CVs, recording accuracy, AUC, and Brier per repeat. Produce (a) a ranked mean table with per-model CIs, (b) a paired heatmap of p-values (all pairs), (c) a stability statement — which model’s variance across repeats is worst and what does that imply for reproducibility of a published winner? This deliverable is the reusable template for every future model-selection question in the course.
C2 (comparison × 3.1.5 AUPRC × 1.3 Bayes). Two hospitals each evaluate your two models; hospital A has 2% disease prevalence, hospital B has 25%. Show empirically that model rankings can flip by metric family (AUC stable, AP and precision@budget flip or compress) across the two prevalences, then write the reporting paragraph that tells both hospitals which model to deploy and why — in language that survives their different baselines.

title: 3.7 Classification Model Comparison
text:
7. Summary

Compare models on identical folds, paired; differences need uncertainty, points don’t settle arguments.
McNemar for hard labels; paired fold differences for scores; replicate for power.
Rank metrics (AUC/AP), probability metrics (Brier, calibration), and operating-point metrics answer different questions — pick per decision, report several.
Calibration is a separate axis: Platt/isotonic fixes on dedicated data; AUC is blind to it, Brier isn’t.
Same tuning budget for every candidate; selection metrics must never double as reported performance.
With several candidates, multiple-comparisons discipline applies — previewing Part 12.
Comparison done honestly is model selection’s foundation: Part 4 formalizes the machinery — starting from why held-out error is the only currency: 4.1 The generalization problem.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text: Classification predicts a categorical response. The output of a classifier is really two things: a score (a probability-like number per case) and a decision rule (a threshold converting scores to labels). Confusing the two is the root of most classification-metric confusion — this page separates them and builds the metric toolkit: confusion matrix, sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall, F1, and ROC.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
1. Basic Concept
Every classifier worth using exposes scores. The confusion matrix tabulates decisions vs truth:




Predicted +
Predicted −




Actually +
TP (hit)
FN (miss)


Actually −
FP (false alarm)
TN (correct rejection)



From it, the quartet that all others are ratios of:
\[\text{Sensitivity/Recall/TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{Specificity/TNR} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\] \[\text{Precision/PPV} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \text{FPR} = \frac{FP}{FP + TN}\]
Accuracy folds everything into one number — and hides everything, too (3.1.5 is dedicated to that trap).






Scores + threshold. Moving the threshold slides cases across the decision boundary — trading recall for precision/specificity along a fixed frontier:






ROC sweeps the threshold and plots TPR against FPR; the area under it (AUC) has a beautiful interpretation — the probability a random positive is scored above a random negative:

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
2. Concept Questions

A screening test has sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.90. In plain words, what do those two numbers promise — and what do they not tell you about a positive result?
Why can accuracy be uninformative while sensitivity/specificity stay excellent? Construct the extreme case.
Your classifier’s scores get monotonically squashed (e.g. all scores squared, order preserved). Which metrics change: accuracy at t = 0.5? AUC? AP?
Precision and recall pull in opposite directions as the threshold moves. State what each one’s denominators “cost” and why no single number captures both.
Two models have identical AUC. Are they interchangeable? Name one axis on which they can differ.



Answers


Promise: 99% of diseased people test positive (few misses); 90% of healthy people test negative. Not promised: that a positive result means disease — that’s PPV, which depends on prevalence (the Bayes result of 1.3: at 0.1% prevalence it’s ~1%… here: 0.99·0.001/(0.99·0.001+0.10·0.999) ≈ 0.98%).
Extreme case: 1% prevalence, “always predict healthy” — accuracy 99%, sensitivity 0. The two class-conditional rates (sensitivity/specificity) are computed within true classes, so they’re immune to prevalence; accuracy isn’t. Report both families or use prevalence-aware metrics.
Squashing destroys the absolute score scale but not the ranking. Accuracy at a fixed threshold can change arbitrarily (t = 0.5 lands somewhere new); AUC is invariant (it uses ranks only); AP likewise (rank-based). Threshold-dependent metrics care about calibration; ranking metrics don’t.
Precision’s denominator (TP+FP) pays for every false alarm the threshold admits; recall’s (TP+FN) pays for every miss. Loosening the threshold admits both more TPs and more FPs — recall ↑, precision typically ↓. Their trade-off is the operating curve; F1 summarizes it at one point, losing the shape.
No — AUC measures ranking quality only. They can differ wildly in calibration (does 0.8 mean 80%?), which matters for cost decisions and downstream probability uses; also in score distribution (threshold placement) and per-region behavior (one may win high-specificity operating points, the other high-sensitivity).

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. From the ranked list below, compute by hand (paper or code, no sklearn) the confusion matrix at threshold 0.5, then TPR/FPR at every possible threshold, the full ROC, and AUC via concordant pairs. Verify every number against sklearn.


Solution







The sweep logic — walk down the ranked list, accumulating hits and false alarms — is the same walk every ROC/PR implementation takes. Owning it once demystifies the curves forever.

Exercise 2. Show the threshold-cost trade in dollars: a screening context has FN cost = $2000 (missed disease), FP cost = $100 (needless follow-up), TN/FN-free = $0. Using the scores from Section 1, compute expected cost at thresholds 0.1–0.9 (step 0.1) and find the cost-optimal threshold. Compare it to the Youden-optimal threshold (max TPR − FPR) and explain when/why the two disagree.


Solution







Youden treats error types symmetrically; real costs almost never are. With FN 20× costlier than FP, the optimal threshold drops (screen loose, confirm hard). Metric choice is a decision-theory choice — there is no threshold-free “best.”

Exercise 3. Cross-validated metric honesty: generate a moderate-signal classification dataset (n = 300, 20% positives), and compare in-sample vs 5-fold-CV values of accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1, and AUC for a logistic classifier. Which metric’s in-sample–CV gap is largest, and why does AUC’s gap behave differently from accuracy’s?


Solution







All in-sample numbers are optimistic; the ranking of metrics is preserved but the gaps differ with each metric’s sensitivity to the specific borderline cases the model tuned on. AUC’s gap tracks the same overfitting — the lesson is not “trust one metric” but “compute every metric out-of-sample,” the discipline Part 4 industrializes.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

confusion_matrix row/column convention: sklearn rows = true, columns = predicted. Transposed matrices are a classic silent error — print it once, label it forever.
AUC pairs with ties count 0.5 (the hand formula above); scores from a coarse model (few distinct values, e.g. a 5-bin risk score) lose AUC resolution through ties.
predict vs predict_proba: predict uses the (possibly inappropriate) 0.5 threshold; decision problems usually want predict_proba + your own threshold from costs (Exercise 2).
Macro vs micro vs weighted averaging of F1 across classes: macro treats a 2% class equally with the 98% class (each class one vote); micro ≈ accuracy. Know which your library reports by default.
AUC ignores calibration — great for ranking, dangerous if someone downstream multiplies your scores into decisions as if they were probabilities; calibration gets its own treatment in 3.7.
Class imbalance doesn’t bias AUC as an estimate of ranking skill, but its sampling noise grows as the positive count shrinks — with 10 positives, one swap changes AUC by 0.02+ (1.4 logic applies to metrics too).


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated evaluation has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fixed version


Accuracy on 2%-positive data is ~98% even for a coin-flip classifier — the number certifies nothing. Use prevalence-aware metrics (recall/precision/F1/AP — see 3.1.5) alongside.
Recall is 0 — the “model” catches no positives at all; the line as printed would show it, but the ‘excellent!’ framing (bug 1) hides the contradiction. Never let one flattering metric sit next to a damning one without comment.
AUC on hard 0/1 predictions throws away the ranking within thresholds — with 0/1 scores, AUC degenerates to balanced accuracy and ties dominate. Feed continuous scores to ranking metrics.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive AUC as the Mann–Whitney U statistic: show that AUC = U/(n₊n₋) where U counts concordant positive-negative pairs (ties as ½), and use this to (a) prove AUC = 0.5 under exchangeable scores, (b) construct the null SD of AUC (≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12·n₊·n₋))) and compute how many positives you need for AUC ± 0.05 at n₋ = 500.


Hint

Each positive-negative pair contributes 1, ½, or 0 to the numerator; under the null each pair is a fair coin.



Solution

By definition of the empirical ROC, each threshold pair (TPR, FPR) increment is (1/n₊, 1/n₋); the area integrates the fraction of pairs with score₊ > score₋ — exactly U/(n₊n₋). (a) Under H₀ (scores exchangeable across labels) each pair is concordant/discordant with probability ½ ⇒ E[AUC] = ½. (b) Var per pair ≈ 1/12 (variance of a fair three-way ±1/½/0 trial scaled); SD(AUC) ≈ √((n₊+n₋+1)/(12n₊n₋)). Setting 1.96·SD ≤ 0.05 with n₋ = 500: n₊ ≈ 1.96²·501/(12·500·0.05²) ≈ 128 positives. Moral: the 10-positive biomarker studies quoted with 3-decimal AUCs are noise — cite the interval, not the point.

Q2. A colleague argues: “We shouldn’t fix the threshold at 0.5; we should report sensitivity and specificity at their best threshold on the test set.” Give the two failures of this plan (optimism and interpretation), then implement the honest version: choose the threshold on a validation split, freeze it, report test-set sensitivity/specificity at the frozen threshold, and compare the two procedures’ reported numbers over 200 resamples.


Solution

Failures: (1) Selection optimism — picking the threshold that maximizes test performance then reporting that same performance is tuning on the test set (0.5); the reported best point is an extreme order statistic, biased upward. (2) Interpretation — the “best” point is noise-selected per dataset; across studies the reported sensitivity/specificity are not the same operating point, so they’re not comparable or replicable. Honest version:






The frozen threshold generalizes; the per-dataset-max procedure would report visibly rosier pairs on average (run both to see the gap). One threshold, chosen where tuning is allowed, applied where it isn’t — the Part 4 ethic in miniature.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (metrics × 1.3 Bayes). A classifier has sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95. Plot PPV as a function of prevalence from 0.1% to 50% (log x-axis). Mark the prevalence at which PPV crosses 50%, and connect the curve to the F1-vs-AP discussion in 3.1.5: which metric family bakes prevalence in, and which keeps it out — and which does your reporting audience actually need?
C2 (metrics × 0.5 Splitting × 4.3 preview). Generate a dataset with 2% positives and fit logistic regression; compute recall at the 0.5 threshold on (a) the full training set, (b) each of 10 stratified CV folds, (c) 10 folds without stratification. Report the spread of recall across folds in (b) vs (c) and tie it to the stratification lessons of 0.5 — then predict what happens to the unstratified recall when prevalence drops to 0.5%.

title: 3.1 Classification Fundamentals
text:
7. Summary

A classifier = scores + threshold; the confusion matrix is where decisions meet truth.
Sensitivity/specificity are prevalence-immune; precision and accuracy are not — know which question each answers.
AUC = probability a random positive outranks a random negative; rank-based, threshold-free, calibration-blind.
Thresholds are decision-theory: costs set them, validation selects them, test sets only measure them.
On imbalanced data, accuracy flatters; balanced accuracy/F1/AP keep you honest.
All metrics inherit sampling noise — small positive counts make small AUC differences meaningless.
When positives get truly rare, even ROC starts flattering: the precision–recall view is next — 3.1.5 AUPRC for skewed datasets.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text: Logistic regression models P(y = 1) as a sigmoid of a linear score — bounded, Bernoulli-likelihood-honest, and the workhorse classifier of applied statistics. Its coefficients speak in log-odds, which is either its greatest interpretive feature or its greatest PR problem, depending on how well you’ve drilled this page.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
1. Basic Concept
The model:
\[p(x) = \frac{e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}}{1 + e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \log\frac{p(x)}{1 - p(x)} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
The logit (log-odds) is linear in x; the sigmoid maps it back to [0, 1]. Coefficients are log-odds ratios: \(e^{\beta}\) multiplies the odds of the outcome per unit of x. Fitting maximizes the Bernoulli log-likelihood — no closed form, solved by iteration (Newton/IRLS):
\[\ell(\beta) = \sum_i \big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - p_i) \big]\]






Note penalty=None: sklearn’s default penalizes the fit (C = 1.0) — worth knowing before comparing coefficients against statsmodels’ unpenalized MLE:






The decision boundary and probability surface, drawn:

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
2. Concept Questions

β = 0.693 for a binary treatment. Translate twice: once into odds, once into a sentence a patient understands.
Where is the decision boundary in terms of the linear score, and why does moving β₀ shift it but moving β₁ rotate it?
sklearn’s default C = 1.0 penalizes coefficients. What happens to the fitted coefficients as C → ∞ and as C → 0, and what real-world failure does the C → 0 extreme prevent?
Logistic regression has no closed-form solution. Why (in one sentence), and what does the algorithm actually optimize?
Your model’s predicted probabilities are well-ranked but poorly calibrated (everything too extreme). Which metric family is blind to this, and what might have caused it?



Answers


Odds multiply by e^0.693 = 2.0 — treatment doubles the odds. For a patient: “if your baseline chance were 1-in-10 (odds 1:9), treatment moves you to about 2-in-9 ≈ 18% chance.” (Odds doubling ≠ probability doubling — the translation must go through the patient’s baseline.)
Boundary = where p = 0.5 = where linear score = 0 (a line, β₀ + β₁x = 0). β₀ shifts the line (offset); β₁ changes its direction/steepness (in 2-D: the normal vector). β₁’s magnitude sets how quickly probability transitions across the boundary.
C → ∞ = no penalty = unpenalized MLE (coefficients as large as likelihood demands); C → 0 = coefficients crushed toward 0 (predicting base rate everywhere). Small C prevents coefficient blow-up under separation or p ≫ n — a ridge penalty in disguise (Part 5).
The log-likelihood is nonlinear in β (β sits inside a sigmoid), so no algebraic zero exists; software maximizes ℓ(β) iteratively — Newton–Raphson/IRLS — the same machinery statsmodels’ summary then reuses for SEs (inverse Hessian).
AUC/AP (3.1, 3.1.5) — rank-based, calibration-blind. Causes: training/serving prevalence mismatch, regularization, resampled training data (oversampling positives), or a drifted population — the fixes live in 3.7’s calibration section.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.


























Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Hand-compute a prediction: given fitted β₀ = −4.0, β₁ = 0.8 (age, in years) for disease status — compute P(disease) at ages 40, 50, 60 by hand (sigmoid), the odds at each age, and verify the odds ratio between consecutive ages equals e^0.8 ≈ 2.23. Then compute the risk ratio between ages 50 and 60 and explain why it differs from the odds ratio.


Solution







The odds ratio is constant (2.23 per 5 years — the model’s defining constraint); the risk ratio depends on the baseline (here ~3.9 at age 60 vs 50). Odds ratios are portable and log-symmetric; risk ratios are what many audiences think they’re hearing — always know which one you quoted.

Exercise 2. The separation problem: construct x where all y = 1 for x > 0 and y = 0 for x < 0 (perfect separation). Fit unpenalized (penalty=None) and watch the coefficients; then fit with C = 0.1 and C = 100. Report coefficient magnitudes, and explain why the MLE “does not exist” here and what the small-C fit is implicitly doing about it.


Solution







Under perfect separation, likelihood increases forever as the slope grows (the model can approach zero training error by steepening the sigmoid) — the MLE diverges to ±∞. The penalty (small C) caps the climb, acting as the prior/regularization that makes the problem well-posed: a finite, conservative boundary. Symptoms in the wild: “convergence warnings” + absurdly large coefficients + predicted probabilities at exactly 0/1 — fix with regularization or better data, not more iterations.

Exercise 3. Logistic regression in a pipeline with honest tuning: build make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)), tune C over a log grid with 5-fold CV (GridSearchCV), and report (a) the chosen C, (b) CV AUC, (c) test AUC on a held-out set, and (d) the odds ratios from the refit model. Then re-run everything with random_state changed — how stable are (a)–(d)?


Solution







Everything is stable to ~a decimal place except C’s exact position on the grid (neighboring Cs perform nearly identically — see the one-standard-error discussion in 4.6). The pipeline guarantees scaling is fit per-fold; the test set answers once, at the end.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

Odds ratios vs risk ratios vs percentage points — three languages for one coefficient. e^β multiplies odds; converting to risk changes requires knowing the baseline (Exercise 1); quoting “30% increase” for e^β = 1.3 is wrong unless p is small.
sklearn penalizes by default — penalty=None (or huge C) for MLE-comparable inference; statsmodels Logit for SEs/p-values. Mixing the two without checking is a silent-model-swap bug.
Regularized coefficients are biased — their SEs are not the inverse-Hessian values; statsmodels-style inference on a penalized fit is invalid (bootstrap if you must).
Separation/quasi-separation → diverging coefficients and zero-width CIs; recognize the convergence warnings, regularize or collect data (Exercise 2).
Complete-data quirks: sklearn’s classes are order-sensitive in coef_ sign conventions; predict_proba[:, 1] is P(class 1) — with string labels, “class 1” is classes_[1], alphabetically determined. Check model.classes_.
Logistic is additive in log-odds — interactions and nonlinearities enter exactly as in Part 2 (2.7, 2.8) but their interpretation happens on the odds scale, which multiplies rather than adds.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated classifier has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Penalized coefficients read as MLE odds ratios: default C = 1 shrinks the coefficient, so the “odds ratio” understates the association. Use penalty=None for interpretable coefficients (or disclose the penalty).
Saturated probabilities described with certainty language: predicted probabilities are never “100% risk” — 0.9997 ≠ certainty; and the 0.5 threshold has no clinical meaning by default. Report ranges and set thresholds from costs (3.1).
Unit-dependent coefficient comparison: multiplying x by 1000 divides the coefficient by 1000 — neither magnitude means anything without units. Standardize (per-SD odds ratios) to compare.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Derive the gradient of the Bernoulli log-likelihood for logistic regression and show it equals \(X^\top (y - p)\) — the same form as linear regression’s normal equations. Two consequences to explain: (a) why Newton–Raphson for logistic = iteratively reweighted least squares, (b) why a perfect-separation dataset makes both the gradient and the Hessian misbehave (relate to Exercise 2).


Hint

ℓ = Σ[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]; dp/dz = p(1−p) with z = x^Tβ; then differentiate ℓ in β via the chain rule.



Solution

With z_i = x_i^Tβ and p_i = σ(z_i): ∂ℓ/∂β = Σ (y_i − p_i) x_i = X^T(y − p). Setting it to zero mirrors OLS’s X^T(y − Xβ) = 0, but p depends on β through sigmoids, so the equation is transcendental — no closed form. Newton–Raphson needs the Hessian H = −X^T W X with W = diag(p(1−p)); the update solves the weighted least-squares problem X^TWX β_new = X^TW z_working — IRLS: iteratively reweighted least squares with working response z = x^Tβ + (y−p)/(p(1−p)). Under separation, as ‖β‖→∞, p_i → 0/1 matching y_i, the gradient X^T(y−p) → 0 along the diverging direction while the log-likelihood itself → its supremum: the iteration drifts to ‖β‖ = ∞ and W’s entries vanish (Hessian degenerates) — numerically rendered as “failure to converge,” statistically as a non-existent MLE.

Q2. LDA vs logistic — the famous equivalence: for two Gaussian classes with shared covariance, both models yield parallel linear boundaries, and their coefficients are proportional. Verify numerically (fit both, compare coefficient directions), then break the equivalence twice — (a) unequal covariances, (b) heavy-tailed features (t-distributed) — and report which model degrades more in each case and why (generative assumption vs discriminative flexibility).


Solution







Equal covariances: directions align (cos ≈ 1) — the two are near-proportional estimates of the same boundary. Unequal covariances: LDA’s shared-covariance assumption is false → its single pooled boundary is mis-specified (QDA is the fix), while logistic, modeling only P(y|x), flexibly fits some linear boundary (though now the Bayes boundary itself is quadratic — both are limited). Heavy tails: LDA’s means/covariances are moment-based and outlier-driven; the logistic likelihood, depending only on y given the score, is typically more robust. Moral (Efron/Friedman): generative models win when their density assumptions hold (faster convergence, fewer parameters); discriminative models are safer when assumptions are questionable.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (logistic × 2.6–2.7). Build a treatment × biomarker model: logit(P(response)) ~ treatment * biomarker_high. (a) Fit and interpret each coefficient in odds-ratio language, including the interaction. (b) Convert the interaction into a difference of log-odds — then show numerically that a positive interaction in log-odds can correspond to a negative difference in absolute risk change at high baselines. What does this imply for presenting “effect modification” to non-statistical audiences?
C2 (logistic × 4.6 Tuning × 1.3 Bayes). Train on a case–control dataset with 50% positives (sampled prevalence ≠ population prevalence of 5%). Show that (unpenalized) logistic regression estimates coefficients consistently but its intercept — hence all predicted probabilities — is miscalibrated by the sampling ratio; correct it with the logit-offset correction (subtract log(sampling odds)) and verify calibration before/after on a population-prevalence test set. This intercept-transport trick is standard in epidemiology and worth owning.

title: 3.3 Logistic Regression
text:
7. Summary

p = σ(linear score): bounded probabilities, Bernoulli likelihood, MLE by IRLS.
Coefficients are log-odds ratios — translate consciously (odds ≠ risk), and standardize before comparing.
sklearn penalizes by default; statsmodels gives unpenalized MLE inference — know which model you fitted.
Separation breaks the MLE; regularization is the practical answer, warnings the tell.
Boundary: score = 0; intercept shifts it, slopes rotate it; probabilities are smooth across it.
Additivity holds in log-odds: interactions multiply odds, not risks — mind the audience.
Discriminating classes without a parametric story is next: 3.4 Generative classifiers (LDA, QDA, Naive Bayes).

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text: The laziest classifier is tempting: encode the classes as numbers (0/1) and run the Part 2 machinery. This page shows precisely what breaks — and the surprisingly defensible uses of the resulting “linear probability model” — so that logistic regression’s logit link (3.3) earns its complexity honestly.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
1. Basic Concept
Fit \(p(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) by OLS on 0/1 outcomes. Three structural problems, none fixable by more data:

Out-of-range predictions: a line is unbounded; probabilities must live in [0, 1]. Near the data’s edges (where decisions matter!) the line exits the unit interval.
Heteroscedasticity by construction: with y ∈ {0,1} and mean p(x), \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) — variance maximal at p = 0.5, vanishing at the extremes (2.10 Q1). Every classical SE is wrong, automatically.
Wrong error family: Gaussian errors on 0/1 outcomes is a category error; the Bernoulli likelihood is the honest one.







The heteroscedasticity signature, live:
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
2. Concept Questions

Why is a predicted probability of −0.2 or 1.3 not merely “slightly wrong” but unusable for decisions built on probabilities?
The heteroscedasticity of the linear probability model is structural. Why can’t a variance-stabilizing transform of y fix it?
For multi-class data encoded 0, 1, 2, what extra assumption does OLS smuggle in beyond the binary case’s problems?
Despite everything, econometricians use linear probability models. Name two properties that make them tolerable in their niche.
Your LPM gives slope 0.06 for a binary predictor. Translate that into the sentence a stakeholder understands.



Answers


Decisions multiply probabilities: expected cost = p × cost; posterior updating; risk thresholds (“treat if p > 0.2”). Negative probability or probability > 1 breaks the arithmetic that decisions are made of — it’s not a small inaccuracy, it’s a type error.
y is 0 or 1; there is nothing to transform (log of 0, arcsine of a constant…). The variance is a function of the mean’s position — only a model whose variance follows the mean (Bernoulli GLM) or robust SEs can cope; no y-transform exists.
Ordinal spacing: coding {control=0, drugA=1, drugB=2} forces the mean response to be linear in the codes — asserting drugB’s effect is exactly double drugA’s and that the categories are ordered at all. Nominal labels have no arithmetic; OLS invents one.

The coefficient is directly interpretable as a percentage-point change in probability per unit x — no odds-ratio translation needed. (b) With mid-range probabilities (0.2–0.8) and modest extrapolation, the line is a decent local approximation, and OLS’s robustness/diagnostics ecosystem applies. (Plus: interaction effects and panel-data fixed-effects machinery are simple in LPM.)

“Moving from the predictor’s 0 to 1 raises the probability of the outcome by 6 percentage points, on average.” (For small probabilities, odds ratios would say something different — this honesty about which summary you’re quoting is the whole game.)
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
3. Drills & Exercises

Drills
Predict, then run.




















Exercises (with solutions)
Exercise 1. Quantify the damage: for the simulation below (steep truth), compute (a) the fraction of the x-range where the LPM predicts outside [0, 1]; (b) the classification error rate of thresholding the LPM at 0 vs 0.5 vs 1 (treating clipped values); (c) the same for clipping predictions into [0,1]. Where does clipping help, where does it silently distort?


Solution







Clipping rescues hard decisions but keeps lying about probabilities — any downstream cost arithmetic (Exercise 2 of 3.1) still consumes nonsense. Classification hides LPM’s sin; probability uses expose it.

Exercise 2. The LPM’s one honest superpower — marginal effects: simulate a logistic truth with modest slope, fit (a) logistic regression and (b) LPM. Compute the logistic model’s average marginal effect (mean over data of dp/dx = p(1−p)·β), and compare it with the LPM slope. Write the sentence explaining why practitioners sometimes prefer the LPM coefficient for reporting.


Solution







For gentle slopes, p(1−p)·β is nearly constant, so “the logistic model’s average effect” ≈ “the LPM slope” — but the LPM gets there with no iteration and reads directly off the coefficient table. That convenience is worth having when the probability range is mid-span; it evaporates near 0 or 1, where the LPM’s line can’t follow the logistic curve.

Exercise 3. Multi-class misuse: simulate three groups with distinct means on x and class labels (control/drugA/drugB) where drugB’s shift is not double drugA’s. Fit OLS on 0/1/2 codes and on one-hot dummies (2.6); show the coded model’s predictions are constrained to a line in code-space while the dummy model’s are not, and quantify the prediction error of each against group means.


Solution







The coded fit is dragged by its fake arithmetic: it must place drugB at exactly twice drugA’s offset. With nominal categories the one-hot model is correct by construction (it’s just group means). Coded-label regression is not a shortcut; it’s a different (wrong) model.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
4. Advanced Information & Pitfalls

The LPM’s coefficient is on the probability scale; logistic’s is on the log-odds scale. Cross-model coefficient comparisons without conversion (e^β, or AMEs) are meaningless — a perennial review-report error.
LPM + HC3 robust SEs fix inference but not the range violations or efficiency losses; it remains an approximation whose quality is a function of how far p sits from 0/1.
Don’t diagnose-and-patch an LPM into a GLM manually — weighting by 1/(p̂(1−p̂)) (“iterated WLS”) is the historical pre-GLM trick; modern practice fits the Bernoulli likelihood directly.
Zero-one-inflated outcomes (p pinned near 0 for most x) make LPM slopes collapse toward 0 and R² meaningless (never above ~prevalence·(1−prevalence)); the rare-event regime is logistic’s home turf.
Thresholding an LPM at 0.5 implicitly equates FP and FN costs — classification thresholds are decision theory (3.1 Exercise 2), not model byproducts.
Why not least squares on probabilities “estimated” from bins? That’s just the binned drill from 2.8 — it works descriptively but has no likelihood, no efficient SEs, and bin boundaries are arbitrary.


Read & Refactor AI Code
This AI-generated model has three bugs. Run, diagnose, fix.








What’s wrong, and the fix


Out-of-range probabilities as deliverables: reporting “P = 1.18” — a number that cannot exist — to stakeholders. Use logistic regression for probability outputs, or at minimum clip-and-disclose (and never feed unclipped values into cost arithmetic).
Classical SEs under structural heteroscedasticity: wrong by construction (2.10 Q1); minimum fix cov_type="HC3", real fix Bernoulli likelihood.
Nominal codes as intensity: “drugB = 2× drugA” was inserted by the encoding, not learned from data (see Exercise 3). Dummies or multinomial logistic, never ordinal codes on nominal labels.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
5. Advanced Questions
Q1. Prove \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon \mid x) = p(x)(1 - p(x))\) for a 0/1 response, and use it to show that OLS’s Gauss–Markov efficiency claim fails for binary data: construct (in simulation) an estimator with lower variance than OLS — e.g., the MLE from logistic regression — and quantify the variance ratio as a function of the probability range in the data.


Hint

Gauss–Markov requires homoscedastic errors; binary data violate it structurally. The Bernoulli MLE is (asymptotically) efficient for its model.



Solution

ε = y − p(x) takes values 1−p (prob 1−p… wait: y=1 w.p. p ⇒ ε = 1−p) and −p (prob 1−p): Var = p(1−p)² + (1−p)p² = p(1−p). Since this varies with x, homoscedasticity fails and OLS is not BLUE for binary data. Simulation:






Wider x-ranges (probabilities pushed toward 0/1, variance collapsing at the extremes) increase the LPM’s relative inefficiency — the Bernoulli MLE exploits the variance function OLS ignores.

Q2. The thresholded-LPM classifier is not insane: threshold the linear fit at 0.5 and it often classifies nearly as well as logistic regression. Construct the regime where they differ maximally (steep sigmoid, wide x-range), show the classification agreement rate, and explain why classification metrics hide what probability metrics expose — connecting to the calibration discussion your 3.1 answer promised.


Solution







Both models place the 0.5-crossing near the same x (monotone scores, same ranking locally), so hard labels agree almost everywhere and accuracy/ROC-type views see little difference. But probability-valued outputs — costs, PPV statements, risk tiers — diverge wildly at the extremes (−0.4 vs 0.03!). Classification metrics are invariant to monotone score warping; probability correctness is not. That’s the calibration axis from 3.1 Q5, and it’s why “same AUC” never means “same model.”
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
6. Complex Questions
C1 (LPM × 2.7 Interaction). In an LPM, interaction coefficients are differences of probability effects — directly interpretable as percentage-point moderation. Fit LPM and logistic (with AME-style interpretation) to the same data with a true interaction; show where the two reports agree (mid-range) and disagree (tail). Which would you present to a clinical audience and why — and what does the “one number per moderation” convenience cost in fidelity at the tails?
C2 (LPM × 3.6 GLMs preview). Write the Bernoulli log-likelihood for data (xᵢ, yᵢ) under (a) the linear-probability model p = β₀+β₁x (where you must clamp/penalize parameter values that push p outside [0, 1]) and (b) the logistic model p = σ(β₀+β₁x). Fit both by direct optimization (scipy.optimize.minimize) and compare each MLE against the plain OLS solution. The punchline to verify: OLS is not even the right fitting criterion for the LPM’s own probabilistic story — report how far apart they land and why.
crumbs: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?

title: 3.2 Why Not Linear Regression for Categories?
text:
7. Summary

OLS on 0/1 labels: unbounded predictions, variance = p(1−p) (heteroscedastic by design), wrong likelihood.
Classification metrics can hide all of this; probability uses and costs expose it.
The LPM survives as a local approximation with direct percentage-point readings — defensible mid-range, dangerous at the tails.
Nominal multi-class labels must never be numerically coded: codes fabricate order and spacing (2.6).
Robust SEs patch inference, not probabilities; clipping patches decisions, not probabilities.
The honest machine for binary responses puts the Bernoulli likelihood and a bounded mean function together — logistic regression: 3.3 Logistic regression.
